steps.text: Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook gently, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and chilli if using, and cook for another minute, stirring, until fragrant.
Pour in the stock and bring to a simmer. Add the broad beans and cook for 5 minutes until just tender.
Add the cicoria (or other greens) and stir well. Simmer for another 8–10 minutes, until the greens are very soft and the beans are completely tender.
Taste and season generously with salt and black pepper.
Ladle into bowls and finish each one with a generous pour of your best olive oil. Serve hot.

notes: If you can't find cicoria, use any bitter greens – dandelion, cavolo nero, kale, or even rocket all work beautifully.
The soup is better the next day when the flavours have had time to sit together. Reheat gently and add the olive oil again when you serve it.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Twice-Cooked Pork
summary: Sichuan's gentler side: tender pork belly with fermented bean paste, peppers and gentle spice.

items.raw: 6 spring onions, whites and greens separated, cut into 3 cm pieces
items.prep: whites and greens separated, cut into 3 cm pieces

items.raw: 1 green capsicum, cut into bite-sized pieces
1 red capsicum, cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Cut the pork belly into thin slices, about 3 mm thick (easier if the pork is slightly cold). Simmer the pork in a pot of water for 20 minutes until just cooked through, then drain and set aside on a plate.
Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a wok or large frying pan over medium heat. Add the spring onion whites, garlic and ginger, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the doubanjiang and stir constantly for 2 minutes, breaking it up as it heats, until the paste darkens slightly and releases its aroma.
Add the cooked pork slices and toss gently but thoroughly, coating each piece in the bean paste, for about 3 minutes.
Add the capsicums, soy sauce, sugar and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring often, for 8 to 10 minutes until the peppers are tender and the sauce is glossy and clingy.
Add the spring onion greens, drizzle with sesame oil, toss once and taste, adjust salt if needed. Serve hot with steamed rice.

notes: You can cook the pork up to a day ahead and refrigerate it, this actually makes slicing cleaner. Reheat gently in the wok before adding the bean paste.
The doubanjiang (or doubanjiang with chilli if you prefer a little more warmth) is your backbone here; don't skip it or use substitutes. It's what makes this dish sing.
Serve with plain steamed rice to balance the rich, umami sauce.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Sakura Ebi and Pea Rice
summary: Fluffy rice with sweet dried shrimp and peas, a Yokohama one-pot that tastes fancy with just four ingredients.

steps.text: Rinse the rice under cold water in a sieve for about 30 seconds, stirring gently, until the water runs almost clear. (This stops it getting gluey.)
Put the rinsed rice, 400 ml water, dried shrimp and salt into a medium rice cooker or a heavy-based pot with a lid. Stir once to combine.

If using a rice cooker, turn it on and close the lid; cook until done (usually 15–18 minutes). If using a pot, bring to the boil over high heat, then reduce heat to low, cover with the lid, and simmer for 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid.
Scatter the frozen peas over the rice (do not stir them in), replace the lid, and cook for a further 2 minutes until the peas are just heated through.
Remove from the heat, let it sit, covered, for 2 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, and the shrimp will have released their sweet flavour right through.
Serve in bowls while warm.

notes: Make sure you don't lift the lid while the rice is cooking, opening it lets the steam out and stops the rice cooking evenly.
This keeps in the fridge for up to three days. Reheat gently in a rice cooker or microwave with a splash of water.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Bagte æg med løg og persillesalat
summary: Creamy baked eggs with caramelised onions and fresh parsley salad.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 large bunch fresh parsley, roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 15 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.
Whisk the eggs together in a bowl with the cream, grated cheese, salt, pepper and thyme. Pour the mixture over the caramelised onions in the pan and stir gently to combine.
Transfer the pan to the oven and bake for 15 to 20 minutes, until the eggs are just set but still a little soft in the centre. It will continue to cook as it cools.
While the æggeost bakes, make the salad: toss the parsley with the olive oil, white wine vinegar, salt and pepper.
Serve the warm æggeost straight from the pan with the fresh parsley salad on the side.

notes: You can stir in sautéed mushrooms or crispy bacon to the eggs before baking if you like.
The æggeost is best served warm, but it's also nice cold for lunch the next day.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Kibbeh
summary: Crispy bulgur and meat fritters shaped by hand, served with yoghurt.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the filling first: heat the olive oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook until soft and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the mince, breaking it up as it cooks, and stir for 5–6 minutes until cooked through. Add the pine nuts, cinnamon and cloves, season with salt and pepper, and stir for another minute. Set aside to cool completely.

Meanwhile, rinse the bulgur under cold water until the water runs clear, then drain well. In a bowl, combine the bulgur, 500 g mince, chopped onion, allspice and cinnamon. Season with salt and pepper. Add cold water a little at a time, mixing with your hands, until the mixture holds together like a dough, you want it moist but not wet. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.

Wet your hands with cold water. Take a handful of the bulgur mixture (about the size of a golf ball) and shape it into an oval. Push your thumb into the centre to make a cavity, then gently hollow it out, rotating it in your palm, until the walls are thin. Fill with about 1 tbsp of the cooled filling, then pinch and seal the opening, gently smoothing the seam. Shape into an oval or pointed torpedo. Repeat with the remaining mixture.

Heat the oil to 160°C in a deep heavy-based pot or wok (use a thermometer to check). Fry the kibbeh in batches, without crowding the pan, for 4–5 minutes, turning halfway, until golden brown and crispy all over. Do not let the oil get too hot or they'll brown before cooking through. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve the kibbeh warm with Greek yoghurt and lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Kibbeh can be shaped up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerated, but don't freeze before frying, the texture gets grainy.
If the mixture is too sticky to work with, add a little more bulgur; if it's too dry, add cold water a teaspoon at a time.
The filling must be completely cool before you stuff, or it will start cooking the shell from inside.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Sate Babi
summary: Balinese pork satay with turmeric and lemongrass, grilled and served with peanut sauce.

items.raw: 600 g pork shoulder, cut into 2 cm cubes
150 g roasted peanuts, crushed or ground

steps.text: Soak the wooden skewers in water for at least 30 minutes.
In a bowl, combine the base genep, pork, palm sugar, fish sauce and coconut oil. Toss well to coat. Cover and marinate in the fridge for 1–24 hours.
Make the peanut sauce: in a bowl, stir together the base genep, crushed peanuts, coconut milk, palm sugar and tamarind paste. Add salt to taste and set aside.
Remove the pork from the fridge 15 minutes before cooking. Drain the skewers. Thread the marinated pork onto the skewers, leaving a small space between each piece.
Heat a grill, grill pan or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the sate for 12–15 minutes, turning every few minutes, until the pork is cooked through (75°C inside) and charred at the edges.
Serve hot with the peanut sauce on the side and lime wedges if you like.

notes: The marinade can be prepared up to 24 hours ahead; overnight is ideal for full flavour.
The peanut sauce can be made earlier in the day and reheated gently before serving.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork until the centre reaches 70°C and the juices run clear.

title: Bánh Mì Thịt Nướng
summary: Charred pork shoulder bánh mì with pickled daikon, coriander and fish sauce mayo on crusty bread.

items.raw: 1 lemongrass stalk, white part only, finely chopped
2 small baguettes (or 1 large baguette), halved lengthways
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Mix fish sauce, palm sugar, garlic, lemongrass and ground coriander in a bowl. Add the pork slices and toss to coat. Let sit for at least 15 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Combine mayonnaise, fish sauce and lime juice in a small bowl, stirring until smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Heat a large frying pan or grill pan over high heat until it's smoking hot. Working in batches if needed, cook the pork until the edges are charred and caramelised, about 2–3 minutes per side. Don't move the pieces around, let them sit so they get a dark, crusty exterior. Set aside on a plate.
Lightly toast the baguette cut-side down in the same hot pan for about 1 minute, until golden and crispy.

Spread the fish sauce mayo on the cut side of each baguette. Layer the charred pork, then pickled daikon, fresh coriander and chilli. Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately while the bread is still warm.

notes: Make the fish sauce mayo and prepare the pickled daikon up to a day ahead; toast the baguette and cook the pork just before eating.
The pork can marinate for up to 2 hours in the fridge for deeper flavour, but 15 minutes is enough for a quick lunch.
If you can't find pickled daikon, use pickled mustard greens or a mix of pickled vegetables, the acid and brightness matter more than the exact vegetable.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety: Cook fresh pork until the centre reaches 70°C and the juices run clear.

title: Bamia
summary: Slow-cooked Iraqi okra and beef stew with tomato, garlic and warming spices.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes
1 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste, cinnamon and cloves, and cook for 1 minute to bloom the spices.

Add the crushed tomatoes and beef stock, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the beef to the pot and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook gently for 40 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender.

Add the okra, salt and pepper. Stir gently to combine. Cover and simmer for a further 30 to 35 minutes, until the beef is very tender and the okra has softened into the sauce. The sauce should be rich, darkened and slightly thickened. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
Serve hot with white rice and lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Bamia freezes beautifully. Cool completely, then freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.
This is even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Make it ahead and warm through before serving.
Some Iraqi cooks add a touch of pomegranate molasses at the end instead of lemon juice, try it both ways and see what you prefer.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Cheat's Bolognese
summary: Freezer-friendly beef mince sauce made with tinned tomatoes and gravy mix, ready in 20 minutes.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the beef mince and break it up as it cooks, stirring often, until browned through, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the carrot and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes and gravy powder, stir well to combine, and bring to a simmer, cooking until the sauce has thickened and turned glossy.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 to 10 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly and the carrot is tender. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Cool completely, then freeze in ice-cube trays. Once frozen, pop the cubes into a freezer bag and label with the date. Thaw and reheat on the stove or stir straight into hot pasta water.

notes: Freeze in ice-cube trays for perfect portion control. One or two cubes is usually enough for a child's serve, three to four for an adult.
Make a double or triple batch and freeze for up to three months. No thawing needed, drop cubes straight into pasta water or a hot pan.
Swap the gravy powder for 1 tsp dried oregano and a splash of Worcestershire sauce if you prefer.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Cook mince, sausages, meatballs and liver right through to 75°C, with no pink in the centre.

title: Tebasaki
summary: Crispy grilled chicken wing tips with salt and pepper, a Fukuoka izakaya staple.

steps.text: Pat the chicken wing tips dry with paper towel.
Season generously with salt and black pepper on both sides.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Place the wing tips skin-side down in the pan. Cook for 6–7 minutes without moving, until the skin is deep golden and crispy.
Flip and cook the other side for 3–4 minutes, until cooked through (meat is no longer pink at the bone).
Transfer to a plate and eat straight away while the skin is still crackling.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Cacio e Pepe
summary: Spaghetti with Pecorino Romano and cracked black pepper.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil, until large bubbles break across the whole surface. The water should taste like the sea.
Toast the cracked pepper in a large, dry frying pan over medium heat for 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant. Add 100 ml of pasta water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cook the spaghetti until al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water before draining.

Add the drained spaghetti to the pan with the pepper water. Remove from heat. Working quickly, add half the grated cheese, tossing constantly with two wooden spoons. Add pasta water a splash at a time, tossing all the while, until the sauce comes together and clings to the pasta. It should be creamy but have no cream in it.
Divide between two bowls. Finish with the remaining cheese and a crack of fresh pepper.

notes: This is a dish about technique, not ingredients. The emulsion of cheese and starch from the pasta water is everything. If your sauce breaks, start again with a little cold water.
Use whole peppercorns and crack them yourself just before cooking, pre-ground pepper will be too fine.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

title: Zaalouk
summary: Warm Moroccan salad of roasted eggplant and tomatoes with garlic and coriander.

steps.text: Preheat your oven to 200°C. Prick each eggplant several times with a fork, then place on a baking tray. Roast for 35–40 minutes, turning halfway, until the skin is blackened and the flesh is very soft.
While the eggplants roast, warm 2 tbsp olive oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant, don't let it brown.
Add the chopped tomatoes to the pan, season with salt and pepper, and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes begin to break down and release their juices.

When the eggplants are soft and charred, remove them from the oven and let cool for a few minutes. Peel away the skin and chop the flesh into small pieces, don't worry about getting it perfect; some texture is good.
Add the eggplant to the tomato pan and stir gently to combine. Cook for 2 minutes to warm through, then taste and adjust the seasoning.

Stir in most of the fresh coriander, reserving some to scatter over the top. Transfer to a serving dish and drizzle with a little extra olive oil. Scatter the remaining coriander over the top and serve warm or at room temperature with bread.

notes: Zaalouk keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days; serve warm or at room temperature.
You can roast the eggplants directly over a gas flame for a more charred, smoky flavour if you prefer, use tongs and turn carefully.
This is traditionally served as part of a mezze spread alongside olives, preserved lemons and bread.

title: Dal with Crispy Onions
summary: Split red lentils cooked soft with spice, topped with crispy fried onions.

steps.text: Heat 1½ tbsp oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they're dark golden and crispy, about 10 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel and set aside.
In a large pot, heat the remaining 1½ tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, cumin and chilli powder. Stir for 30 seconds to bloom the spices.

Add the lentils, water (or stock) and crushed tomatoes. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have broken down and the dal is creamy, about 25 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
Spoon the dal into bowls and top with the crispy onions. Scatter with fresh coriander if you like.

title: Makroudh
summary: Tunisian semolina cookies with dates and orange blossom, crispy outside and tender inside.

items.raw: 100 g softened butter, cut into small pieces

steps.text: Make the filling first: melt the 60 g butter in a saucepan over low heat. Add the dates and stir constantly, breaking them down with the back of a wooden spoon, until they form a smooth paste, about 5 minutes. Stir in the orange blossom water and salt, then set aside to cool.

For the dough: put the semolina, baking powder and salt in a bowl. Add the softened butter pieces and rub together with your fingertips until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs. Add the orange blossom water and warm water, a little at a time, mixing gently until the dough comes together, it should feel soft and slightly moist but not sticky. Knead lightly for 1 minute.

Lightly oil your work surface. Take a piece of dough about the size of a walnut and flatten it into a disc about 5 mm thick. Place a teaspoon of date paste in the centre, fold the dough in half over the filling, then pinch the edges firmly to seal. You can press it gently with the tines of a fork to make ridges if you like. Repeat with the remaining dough and filling, you should make about 12 cookies.

Heat the neutral oil in a deep saucepan to 180°C (a piece of dough should sizzle immediately and turn golden in about 30 seconds). Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the makroudh until they're deep golden brown all over, about 2–3 minutes, turning halfway through. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them to a paper-towel-lined plate.
While they're still warm, brush or drizzle the warmed honey lightly over each makroudh. Let them cool for a few minutes on the paper towels, they'll crisp up as they cool.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days. They stay crispy at room temperature.
Don't skip the honey, it's traditional and brings everything together. Just a light coating is enough.
If you want to make these ahead, you can prepare the dough and filling the day before and assemble and fry them on the day.

title: Asado de Tira
summary: Argentine grilled short ribs, charred and tender, the heart of Sunday family gatherings.

items.raw: 1.5 kg beef short ribs (asado de tira), cut into 3-rib portions

steps.text: Make the chimichurri first: combine the parsley, oregano, garlic and chilli in a bowl. Pour in the olive oil and red wine vinegar, then stir and taste. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside for at least 30 minutes, or up to 1 hour, to let the flavours come together.
Light your charcoal or wood fire 30–40 minutes before you want to grill. You need a good bed of hot coals for the asado to char properly on the outside while staying tender inside.
When the fire is ready and glowing, pat the ribs dry and season generously all over with salt and pepper on both sides. Let them sit for 5 minutes.
Place the ribs on the grill with the bone side facing the heat first, about 15–20 cm from the coals. Grill for 12–15 minutes until golden and charred, then turn to the meat side.
Cook the meat side for another 12–15 minutes, keeping a close eye for an even char. The meat should be tender when you press it with a fork, and the internal temperature should reach 65°C for medium.
If the outside is charring too fast before the inside is done, move the ribs further from the heat for the last few minutes.
Transfer the ribs to a warm platter and rest for 5–10 minutes. Pour the chimichurri over the top, or serve it alongside so everyone can add as much as they like.
Serve warm with crusty bread to soak up every drop of chimichurri and meat juices.

notes: Chimichurri can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept at room temperature.
Asado de tira is best cooked over charcoal or hardwood fire. If using a gas grill, preheat to high heat and cook for the same time, checking for tenderness.
Internal temperature for medium is 65°C. For a softer, more melting texture, cook to 68°C.
Food safety: Wash fresh produce well, refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat them within 3 days.

title: Salsa Roja
summary: Simple cooked red sauce of tomatoes, chillies and garlic for tacos.

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan or comal (or frying pan if that's what you have) over medium-high heat. Work in batches if needed: char the tomatoes, turning occasionally, until soft and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Set aside.
In the same pan, char the red chillies and garlic cloves until soft and blistered, about 3 minutes. Add to the tomatoes.
Add the onion to the pan and cook until soft and lightly coloured, about 3 minutes.
Transfer the tomatoes, chillies, garlic and onion to a blender. Blend until smooth or to your preferred texture, some people like it chunky.
Return the salsa to the pan and simmer over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it's thick and the flavours have come together.
Season with salt to taste. Serve warm or at room temperature with tacos, quesadillas or whatever you're cooking.

notes: Make it ahead: this keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze it for a month.
No blender? Mash it with a fork or stick blender in the pan.
If you can't get red chillies, use jalapeños, or even a pinch of chilli powder, it's still salsa.

title: Rendang Daging
summary: Slow-cooked beef rendang, rich with coconut and spices.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 4 cm pieces

steps.text: Blitz the red chillies, garlic, ginger and shallots in a food processor to a smooth paste, adding a splash of water if needed.

Heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a heavy pot or large saucepan over medium-high heat. Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the beef until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the paste to the same pot and fry, stirring often, until fragrant and the oil starts to separate, about 4 minutes.
Add the ground coriander, cumin and turmeric, stirring for 1 minute until toasted.

Pour in the coconut milk and stir in the tamarind paste. Return the beef to the pot along with the makrut lime leaves. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low and cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, for about 1 hour. The rendang is ready when the beef is very tender and the sauce has thickened and darkened.
Taste and add salt as needed. The coconut oil should be rich and glossy on top. Serve hot with steamed rice.

notes: Make this a day ahead, the flavours deepen overnight and the beef becomes even more tender. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if the sauce is too thick.
If you prefer a hotter rendang, add extra red chillies to the paste, or finely chop a bird's eye chilli to stir in at the end.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice and a cool cucumber sambal to cut through the richness.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Pad Krapow Gung
summary: Stir-fried prawns with holy basil and garlic over rice.

items.raw: 200 g king prawn, peeled and deveined
1 long red chilli, sliced (or 2 birds eye chilli if you want serious heat)
items.note: or 2 birds eye chilli if you want serious heat

items.raw: Large handful fresh Thai basil, leaves only

steps.text: Heat the wok over high heat until it's smoking. Add the oil and swirl.
Add the garlic and stir constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant and just starting to colour.
Add the prawns and toss for 1 minute, then add the fish sauce and sugar. Keep stirring until the prawns are pink and cooked through, about 2–3 minutes.
Add the chilli and toss for 30 seconds.
Pull the wok off the heat, scatter the basil leaves over the top and toss gently through (the heat will wilt them).
Pile on to a plate of jasmine rice and eat straight away.

notes: Prep everything before you start cooking, there's no time once the wok is hot.
If you can't find king prawns, use medium prawns (just reduce the cooking time by 30 seconds).
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Wambatu Curry
summary: Creamy eggplant curry with coconut milk and warming spices, a Sunday staple.

items.raw: 700 g eggplant, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger, stir well, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add curry powder and turmeric, stir to coat the onions, and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add eggplant cubes and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and water. Add the green chillies and season with salt.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 15 to 18 minutes, until the eggplant is tender and the curry has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot with rice.

notes: This curry tastes even better the next day. Cool and store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to a month.
Dilan brings this to work in a thermos flask for night shifts, it keeps beautifully and reheats gently.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Bush Tomato Lamb Stew
summary: Slow-cooked lamb with native bush tomato, a tangy Central Australian native ingredient.

items.raw: 1.5 kg lamb shoulder, cut into 4 cm chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or camp oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.
Add the onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and beginning to colour, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

Return the lamb to the pot along with the carrot, tinned tomatoes, dried bush tomato, beef stock and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook gently for 2 to 2½ hours, until the lamb is very tender, stirring occasionally. If using a camp oven, place over coals at a low heat.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Keeps in the fridge for 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
If you can't find dried bush tomato at your local grocer, look for it at farmers markets or Aboriginal-owned food suppliers.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Pepper Sauce
summary: Rohan's fiery Trinidadian hot sauce of Scotch bonnets, coriander and mustard.

steps.text: Put the Scotch bonnets, coriander, mustard, garlic, lime juice and a pinch of salt into a blender.
Blitz until smooth, about 1 minute.
Taste and add more salt or lime juice if needed.
Transfer to a jar and refrigerate until ready to use.

notes: Keep in a jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.
For a smoother sauce, peel the chillies first. For more texture, pulse instead of blitzing.
Add a little water if it's too thick.

title: Low Country Red Rice
summary: Tomato-stained rice with bacon and onions, cooked in cast iron the Low Country way.

steps.text: Heat a cast iron frying pan over medium heat. Cook the bacon until crispy, about 5 minutes, then transfer to a plate, leaving the fat in the pan.
Add the onion to the bacon fat and cook, stirring often, until soft and starting to caramelize, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the rice and cook for 1 minute, coating it in the fat.
Add the crushed tomatoes, stock, salt, pepper and cayenne (if using). Stir well, then bring to a gentle simmer until small bubbles break the surface.
Cover and cook for 20 minutes without lifting the lid, until the rice is tender and has absorbed the liquid.
Remove from heat, stir in the cooked bacon, and let it rest for 2 minutes before serving.

notes: Serves well alongside shrimp, sausage or collard greens.
Can be made a day ahead and reheated gently on the stove with a splash of stock.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Matzo Ball Soup
summary: Grandmother's golden broth with fluffy matzo balls, the ultimate Jewish comfort food.

items.raw: 2 kg chicken bones (or whole chicken pieces)
3 celery stalks, cut into 5 cm chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the broth: place chicken bones in a large pot, cover with 3 litres of cold water, and bring to a boil. Skim off any grey foam that rises to the surface, about 2 minutes.

Add the onions, carrots, celery, parsnip (if using), parsley and bay leaf. Reduce heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 1½ to 2 hours. The broth should be clear and golden. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

While the broth simmers, make the matzo balls: beat the eggs with oil and soda water until combined. Stir in the matzo meal, salt, white pepper and ginger (if using) until just mixed, the batter will be thick and slightly chunky. Cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil until it is at a steady rolling boil (use a separate pot so it doesn't interfere with your broth simmering). With cold, wet hands, gently roll the matzo batter into balls about 4 cm in diameter. Place them on a wet plate as you go.

Carefully drop the matzo balls into the boiling water one at a time. They will sink, then float to the surface after a few minutes. Once they float, simmer them gently for 30 minutes, do not let them boil hard or they'll become tough.

Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the vegetables and bones. Return to a clean pot and gently reheat. Carefully transfer the matzo balls to serving bowls and ladle the golden broth over them. Serve hot.

notes: The broth can be made up to 3 days ahead and stored in the fridge, or frozen for up to 3 months. Matzo balls can be cooked and frozen separately for up to 1 month.
For a lighter broth, use chicken breasts instead of bones; reduce cooking time to 45 minutes. For richer broth, add extra chicken fat (schmaltz) when serving.
The soda water is key to light, fluffy matzo balls, don't skip it. And cold hands matter more than you'd think; it keeps the batter from getting tough.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches 75°C and the juices run clear, with no pink meat near the bone.

title: Barbacoa
summary: Slow-cooked beef brisket wrapped in agave leaves, shredded until tender for tacos.

items.raw: Agave leaves (or banana leaves), for wrapping

steps.text: Heat the oven to 120°C. Toast the dried guajillo and chipotle chillies in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant, then transfer to a bowl and cover with hot water. Let sit for 15 minutes until soft.

Drain the rehydrated chillies, then blitz them in a blender with garlic, cumin, oregano, cloves, beef stock, vinegar and salt until smooth. Strain through a sieve if you want a silky paste; for rustic texture, leave it coarse.
Pat the brisket dry. Rub all over with the chilli paste until well coated. Wrap tightly in agave or banana leaves and then in foil, sealing the edges.
Place the wrapped brisket in a heavy-based pot or Dutch oven. Cover and braise in the oven for 7 to 8 hours, until the meat shreds easily with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 15 minutes. Unwrap carefully, watch out for steam, and shred the beef using two forks, pulling it apart along the grain.
Strain the braising liquid into a jug. Skim any fat from the surface and season with salt to taste. Toss the shredded beef with a few tbsp of the braising liquid to keep it moist.

notes: Make ahead: cook the barbacoa the day before, then shred and reheat gently in the braising liquid. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Serve on warm flour tortillas with diced onion, fresh coriander and lime wedges.
This is a weekend cook: take your time and let the low heat do the work.
Food safety: Slow-cooked meat is safe once it is tender and the centre has reached at least 75°C. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Bariis iyo Caano
summary: Broken rice cooked soft with milk and cardamom, a comforting Somali breakfast.

items.raw: 250 g broken rice (or short-grain white rice, lightly crushed)
items.note: or short-grain white rice, lightly crushed

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a large pot over medium heat. Add the crushed cardamom pods and warm until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the broken rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes, toasting it lightly.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring often, until the water is mostly absorbed, about 10 minutes.
Reduce the heat to low and pour in the milk slowly, stirring as you go. The rice will be creamy but still soft, not stiff.
Cook gently, stirring every 2 minutes, until the rice is very soft and the mixture is thick and porridgy, about 12 minutes. Add salt to taste.
If it's too thick, add a splash of warm milk. Serve hot in bowls.

notes: Make it ahead and reheat gently with a splash of milk, it keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
If you can't find broken rice, crush short-grain white rice coarsely with your hands or a rolling pin before cooking.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Ajiaco Colombiano
summary: Hearty potato and chicken soup with corn and cream, comfort in a bowl.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken thighs, bone-in and skin-on
400 g floury potato, cut into chunks
200 g sweet potato, cut into chunks
2 corn cobs, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the chicken thighs, onion quarters and crushed garlic into a large pot. Cover with the chicken stock and bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer gently for 15 minutes. Skim off any foam that rises to the top.
Add the floury and waxy potatoes to the pot. Simmer for another 10 minutes until they start to soften.
Add the sweet potato and corn pieces. Continue to simmer for 8–10 minutes until all the potatoes are tender and the corn is cooked through.
Remove the chicken thighs and set aside to cool slightly. Once cool enough to handle, shred the meat into bite-sized pieces, discarding the skin and bones.
Return the shredded chicken to the pot. Stir in the cream and season with salt and pepper to taste. Heat through gently without boiling.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with fresh coriander if you have it on hand.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Blackened Catfish
summary: Catfish fillets crusted with Cajun spices and seared hard in a cast-iron frying pan until smoky and crispy.

steps.text: Mix paprika, cayenne, cumin, onion powder, garlic powder, thyme, oregano, black pepper and salt in a shallow dish.
Pat the catfish fillets dry with paper towels. Coat both sides generously with the spice mixture, pressing it on so it sticks.
Heat the oil in a cast-iron frying pan over high heat until it's smoking and a drop of water beads and rolls across the surface, about 2 minutes.
Add the butter and swirl it through the hot oil. When it's foaming and just starting to brown, lay the catfish fillets in the frying pan, they should sizzle hard.
Sear without moving them for 3 to 4 minutes, until the crust is dark brown and charred. Flip carefully.
Sear the other side for another 2 to 3 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily with a fork. Serve hot.

notes: Serve with white rice, collard greens or a simple slaw to cool the heat.
The frying pan must be smoking hot, don't skip this step or you won't get that proper blackened crust.
Swap catfish for any firm white fish fillet.
Food safety: Cook fish until it turns opaque and flakes easily, about 63°C in the thickest part.

title: Kopytka
summary: Little potato and flour dumplings tossed with caramelized onions and mushrooms.

items.raw: 500 g floury potato, peeled and halved
2 brown onions, sliced into thin rings

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and pass through a ricer while still hot into a large bowl.
Add the flour, egg, and salt to the potato. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, it should feel a little soft and slightly sticky, not smooth. Don't overwork it.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Dust the work surface lightly with flour. Break off a piece of dough about the size of a walnut, roll it roughly into a stick about 5 cm long, and press gently with your thumb to make a small indent (this is the little hoof). Drop each kopytka into the boiling water as you shape them. They will sink, then float to the surface; cook for 2–3 minutes after they float. Drain and spread on a tray to cool.

While the kopytka cook, heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and fry, stirring often, until they are golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 8 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium and add the onions to the same pan. Cook, stirring now and then, until they are soft and deeply golden, about 12 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme, if using, and cook for another minute.
Return the mushrooms to the pan with the onions. Add the drained kopytka and toss gently until everything is warm and coated. Season with salt and black pepper. Serve hot.

notes: Kopytka can be made ahead: shape and boil them, then store in the fridge for up to 2 days. Toss with the mushrooms and onions to warm through.
The dough should stay slightly loose, too much flour and the kopytka become heavy. If it's very sticky, dust with a little more flour, but resist the urge to knead.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Atole de Chocolate
summary: Thick, creamy corn masa drink with Oaxacan chocolate and cinnamon, warm for breakfast.

items.raw: 250 g fresh masa (corn dough), or masa harina mixed with warm water
items.prep: or masa harina mixed with warm water

items.raw: 100 g Oaxacan chocolate (tableta), chopped (such as de agua o de metate)
items.note: tableta; such as de agua o de metate

steps.text: In a heavy-based pot, heat the water and milk together over medium heat until steaming but not boiling, about 5 minutes.
In a small bowl, whisk the fresh masa with 1 cup of the warm liquid to dissolve it completely, breaking up any lumps. (If using masa harina, mix it with the liquid until smooth.)
Pour the masa mixture slowly into the pot, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Add the cinnamon stick.
Continue stirring over medium heat until the mixture thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 8 minutes.
Add the chopped chocolate and sugar. Stir well until the chocolate is completely melted and the atole is smooth and frothy.
Taste and adjust sugar and salt as needed. Remove from heat.
If you have a molinillo (traditional wooden whisk), hold the pot and roll the molinillo between your palms to make the atole frothy and light. Otherwise, whisk vigorously for a minute.
Serve hot in bowls or mugs, and drink while it's warm.

notes: Fresh masa is best, but masa harina (corn flour) works well too: use about 125 g mixed with a little warm water to a smooth paste.
Oaxacan chocolate is grainy and textured, sold as tablets, seek it in Latin or Mexican markets, or use good dark chocolate with a tiny pinch of ground almond added.
A molinillo whisk creates the traditional frothy top, but a regular whisk does the job.

title: Rajas Poblanas
summary: Roasted poblano strips in a creamy sauce with jalapeños, onion and cheese.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Hold each poblano over a gas flame or under a hot grill, turning with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over, about 3–4 minutes per chilli. Place in a plastic bag for 5 minutes to steam, then peel away the blackened skin under cool running water.
Slit each poblano lengthwise and gently remove the seeds and white membrane, keeping the chilli in one piece. Cut the roasted poblanos lengthwise into 1 cm strips.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and diced jalapeño, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the cream and stir through the cheese until melted and the sauce is smooth, about 2 minutes. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Gently fold the poblano strips into the sauce and warm through for 2–3 minutes. Serve hot as a main or side dish.

notes: Rajas poblanas can be served as a main dish with warm tortillas, or as a side to grilled vegetables or eggs.
If you cannot find poblanos, use large green capsicums; they will be milder but the dish still works well.

title: Khoresh Rivas
summary: Rhubarb and lamb stew, spring's tart grace over rice with tahdig

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 3 cm pieces
1 large brown onion, halved and sliced
400 g fresh rhubarb, cut into 4 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the turmeric and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the lamb to the pot. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat. Pour in the stock, bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the rhubarb pieces and season with salt and pepper. Continue to simmer, covered, for another 30 minutes. The rhubarb should soften and break down slightly, and the lamb should be tender. The stew will taste sharp and rich. Taste and adjust seasoning.

While the stew cooks, prepare the rice. Rinse the basmati rice in a sieve under cold running water until the water runs clear. Bring 1 litre of salted water to a boil in a separate pot. Add the rice and stir gently. Boil for about 10 minutes, until the rice is just tender but still has a slight bite. Drain well.

Return the drained rice to the pot. Drizzle 2 tbsp of oil or melted butter over the rice and gently fold it in. Make a well in the centre of the rice. Mix the yoghurt (if using) with 1 tbsp oil and spread on the bottom of a small bowl or saucer to place in the well, this helps the tahdig form. Cover the pot tightly with foil, then place the lid on top.

Cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes. You should hear a gentle sizzle and smell the toasted rice. This is the tahdig forming. Lower the heat to the lowest setting and cook for another 10 minutes.
To serve, spoon the rice onto a platter, breaking up the tahdig gently from the bottom of the pot and scattering it over the top. Pour the khoresh over and around the rice. Serve hot.

notes: The khoresh tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently before serving.
If you can't find fresh rhubarb, use frozen; no need to thaw. The stew will be slightly thinner and more sour.
The tahdig is forgiving. If it burns black, you've learned something for next time. If it doesn't form at all, the stew is still worth eating.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Mì Xào Rau Muống
summary: Stir-fried wheat noodles with water spinach, garlic and ginger, simple temple food, weeknight done well.

items.raw: 400 g fresh wheat noodles (or dried, cooked and cooled)
400 g water spinach (rau cần), cut into 5 cm lengths
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: If using dried noodles, cook in boiling salted water until just tender, drain well and spread on a tray to cool. Fresh noodles can be used as they are.
Heat the oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over high heat. When shimmering, add the sliced garlic and ginger. Stir-fry for about 1 minute until fragrant but not brown.
Add the water spinach and toss constantly for 2–3 minutes until it begins to wilt but the stems still have a gentle firmness.
Add the cooled noodles to the wok, breaking them apart gently with chopsticks or tongs as you toss. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until heated through.
Pour the soy sauce and rice vinegar over the noodles and toss well for another minute, letting the flavours coat everything evenly.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. If you like heat, sprinkle with dried chilli flakes.
Serve at once, while the noodles are still warm and the spinach stems hold their slight crispness.

notes: If water spinach is hard to find, use baby bok choy or broccolini cut into shorter lengths; they cook in the same time.
The noodles should be completely cool before stir-frying so they don't clump and stick together.

title: Granita di Mandorla
summary: Icy almond milk drink with a brioche, how Sicilians really start the day.

steps.text: Pour the water into a bowl and add the ground almond. Stir well to combine, breaking up any lumps. Let sit for 10 minutes so the almond releases its flavour and begins to soften.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve or muslin cloth, pressing gently to extract all the almond milk. Discard the solids (or save them for baking if you wish).
Stir the caster sugar, milk and vanilla extract into the almond milk until the sugar dissolves completely. Taste and add a pinch of salt to enhance the almond flavour.
Pour into a shallow freezer container and freeze, stirring with a fork every 30 minutes for the first 3 hours to create a slushy, granular texture. Then leave undisturbed overnight until firm.
To serve, scoop the granita into glasses. Top with a little cold milk if you like, and serve with a brioche bun on the side for dunking.

notes: Granita keeps well in the freezer for up to a week. Scoop it out as needed; if it hardens too solid, let it sit at room temperature for 5 minutes before serving.
For a richer granita, use equal parts almond milk and full-cream milk in the base instead of water and milk.
Some Sicilians make a thinner granita by adding a splash more milk at serving time. Do whatever feels right to you.

title: Mackerel Rundown
summary: Mackerel cooked down in coconut broth with green bananas and yam.

items.raw: 2 fresh mackerel, cleaned and cut into chunks
1 green banana, peeled and cut into chunks
200 g yam, peeled and cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook, stirring, until soft and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Add the mackerel chunks and cook for 2 minutes on each side to seal them, then remove and set aside.

Pour the coconut milk into the pot and stir well to mix with the onion and garlic. Add the green banana and yam chunks, and drop in the whole scotch bonnet if using (it will flavour the broth without breaking apart).

Return the mackerel to the pot and add the dried thyme. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 20 to 25 minutes, until the banana and yam are tender and the mackerel is cooked through.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. If you used the whole chilli and want more heat, carefully break it open and stir in the seeds. Stir in the spring onions and cook for 1 minute more.
Ladle into bowls, making sure each serves gets fish, vegetables and plenty of broth.

notes: Make it a day ahead if you like, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove.
The scotch bonnet stays whole while cooking so you control the heat. Leave it out if you prefer a gentler dish.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Ezogelin Çorbası
summary: Light Turkish lentil soup with bulgur, tomato and warming spices.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato paste, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Stir in the lentils and bulgur, coating them with the oil. Add the cumin and dried mint, stirring to combine.

Pour in the tinned tomatoes and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the lentils and bulgur are tender and the soup is creamy, about 25–30 minutes.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper as needed.
Ladle into bowls and top with fresh mint or parsley if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: this soup keeps well in the fridge for 3 days, and the flavours deepen as it sits. Reheat gently with a splash of water or stock if it's too thick.
For extra depth, add a splash of red wine vinegar or lemon juice just before serving.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Steak and Ale Pudding
summary: Beef and ale filling in suet pastry, steamed in a pudding basin, proper old-school comfort.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Season the beef with salt and pepper. Brown the meat in batches, about 3 minutes per batch, until well coloured on all sides. Set aside.
In the same pan, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes more.

Return the beef to the pan. Pour in the ale and stock, scraping the bottom of the pan. Add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then remove from heat and leave to cool completely, at least 1 hour. The filling needs to be cold before you add it to the pastry.

While the filling cools, make the suet crust. Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl. Add the suet and stir until it's distributed evenly. Add the cold water a little at a time, stirring with a knife until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead gently until just combined; don't overwork it.

Lightly flour a work surface. Roll out two-thirds of the dough into a circle about 40 cm across and 5 mm thick. It should be large enough to line a 1.5-litre pudding basin with some hanging over the edge.
Use this large circle to line the pudding basin, leaving the excess hanging over the rim.

Strain the cooled filling, reserving the liquid. Discard the bay leaves and thyme. Spoon the beef and onions into the lined basin, then pour in enough of the reserved liquid to come halfway up the filling (about 200 ml). Save the rest for serving.
Roll out the remaining dough into a circle about 25 cm across, 5 mm thick. Lay this on top of the filling. Fold the overhanging pastry inward over the lid, pressing down to seal.
Cover the pudding with a pleated piece of baking paper (the pleat allows for expansion), then a pleated piece of foil. Tie both down with string under the lip of the basin.

Place the pudding basin in a large pot and add enough boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover the pot with a lid. Steam for 3 hours, checking every 45 minutes and topping up the water if needed, it should stay at the same level.
Carefully remove the pudding from the pot. Let it rest for 10 minutes. Warm the reserved liquid in a small pan.
Turn the pudding out onto a warm plate or serving bowl. Serve with the warmed gravy poured over the top, and mashed potato on the side.

notes: If you don't have a pudding basin, a 1.5-litre heatproof bowl wrapped in foil will work, though you may need to adjust the steaming time slightly.
Leftovers can be reheated gently in the steamer for 30 minutes, or covered in foil in a 150°C oven for about 45 minutes.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Semlor
summary: Soft cardamom buns filled with almond paste and whipped cream, a Swedish fika favourite.

steps.text: Mix the warm milk, yeast and a pinch of the caster sugar in a bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.

Add the remaining caster sugar, softened butter, salt, cardamom and egg yolk. Stir well, then gradually work in the flour until a soft dough forms. Knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should be slightly sticky.
Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a clean tea towel, and leave to rise in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until doubled in size.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured bench and divide into 8 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, place on baking trays lined with baking paper, cover loosely, and leave to prove for 30–40 minutes until puffy.
Preheat the oven to 200°C. Brush each bun with beaten egg, then bake for 12–15 minutes until golden and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Once cool enough to handle, carefully slice the top third off each bun and set aside. Scoop out a small amount of crumb from inside each bun to make room for the filling.
Mix the almond meal, icing sugar and water to a paste. Divide evenly among the buns, spooning into the cavity.
Whip the cream with the caster sugar until soft peaks form. Top each bun with a generous dollop of cream, then replace the lid at an angle.
Serve at room temperature the same day.

notes: Make the dough the day before if it suits you, cold dough ferments gently overnight. Shape and prove the next morning.
If you grind whole cardamom pods yourself, use about 1½ tsp of pods; they're more fragrant than pre-ground.
Semlor are best eaten the day they're made. Store in an airtight container for up to a day, but the bun will soften.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Sandesh
summary: Cardamom-scented cottage cheese sweet, the Bengali classic at the heart of a thousand gentle arguments.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a rolling boil in a heavy-bottomed pan over high heat, until it foams up and rises towards the rim. Once it reaches a full boil, remove from the heat.

Add the yoghurt slowly, stirring gently. The milk will curdle immediately. Let it sit for 2 minutes, then pour through a fine sieve lined with muslin cloth, collecting the whey in a bowl beneath. Let it drain for 5 minutes.
Gather the corners of the muslin and hang it to drain for 30 minutes until the paneer is quite dry but still soft.

Turn the paneer into a bowl and crumble it finely with your fingertips. Add the khoya, sugar, cardamom seeds (discarding the husks), and salt. Mix gently but thoroughly until the mixture just holds together.
Divide the mixture into 12 portions and shape each into a small smooth ball or oval with damp hands. You can press each into a small mould if you have one, then tap it out onto a plate.
Chill for at least 15 minutes before serving. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

notes: If you can't find khoya, reduce 500 ml milk slowly in a heavy pan until it becomes a thick paste (about 30 minutes), then use that instead, it will give you more authentic flavour and texture.
For a softer sandesh (Arnab's preference), use only 50 g khoya and don't chill for as long; for a firmer set (his wife's way), add an extra 25 g khoya.
Regional variations: try adding a few strands of saffron, a tablespoon of mango pulp, or a teaspoon of rose water instead of cardamom, the arguments are endless and that's rather the point.

title: Seezunge Müllerin Art
summary: Pan-fried sole with brown butter and lemon, a Northern German classic.

items.raw: 2 whole sole (300–350 g each), gutted and cleaned
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the sole dry with paper towels. Season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Spread the flour on a shallow plate. Lightly coat both sides of each fish, shaking off the excess.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Lay the sole in the pan and cook, without moving, for 2–3 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes until cooked through.
Transfer the fish to a warm plate. Reduce the heat to medium, add the butter to the same pan, and let it melt and brown, swirling gently, for 1–2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns golden.
Pour the brown butter over the fish, squeeze lemon juice over the top (it will sizzle briefly), scatter with parsley if using, and serve at once while the butter is still hot and nutty.

notes: Sole is the classic choice, but halibut, plaice or any firm white fish works. You can also cook fillets, they'll need only 1–2 minutes per side.
The brown butter is everything. Don't skip it or rush it; the aroma tells you when it's ready.

title: Dolma
summary: Grape leaves stuffed with herbed rice and meat, slowly simmered until tender.

items.raw: 400 g jarred grape leaves, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.

Add the lamb mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned, about 8 minutes. Stir in the rice, mint, parsley, cumin and allspice. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and cool slightly.

Lay a grape leaf flat, shiny side down, on a clean surface. Place 1 tbsp of filling near the base of the leaf. Fold the sides in, then roll tightly from the base towards the tip, tucking in the sides as you go. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling.
Line the base of a heavy pot with any remaining or torn grape leaves. Arrange the dolma seam-side down, snugly packed in a single layer (or two layers if needed).
Pour the stock around the dolma. Drizzle with the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Place a plate or small lid directly on the dolma to keep them submerged.
Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce heat to low. Cook, uncovered, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the rice is tender and the leaves are soft. The stock will reduce and mostly be absorbed.
Let rest for 5 minutes, then serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make ahead: Roll the dolma up to 1 day ahead and store in the fridge. Cook just before serving.
Room temperature: These are just as good served at room temperature the next day, making them perfect for packed lunches.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Cook mince, sausages, meatballs and liver right through to 75°C, with no pink in the centre.

title: Soupe à l'Oignon
summary: Silky onion soup with fish stock and dark caramelized onions, Dakar comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they soften and begin to release their moisture, about 10 minutes.

Continue cooking the onions, stirring occasionally, until they are deeply caramelized and golden brown, about 30–40 minutes. This takes patience, but it's where all the flavour comes from. Lower the heat if they start to catch.
Add the chopped garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the fish stock and add the bay leaf. Bring to a simmer, then lower the heat and cook gently for about 5 minutes to let the flavours meld.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Remove the bay leaf.
Ladle into deep bowls and serve hot. Tear in crusty bread if you like, and let it soften into the soup.

notes: For extra richness, some cooks stir in a spoonful of crème fraîche or Greek yoghurt just before serving.
Make this ahead and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Kalua Pork
summary: Slow-roasted Hawaiian pork, tender enough to shred with a fork, seasoned the island way.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 160°C. Pat the pork shoulder dry with paper towels.
Mix salt, pepper and crushed garlic together. Rub the mixture all over the pork, getting it into any cracks in the skin.
Line a large roasting pan with banana leaves (or just use the pan). Place the pork skin-side up on the leaves. Cover tightly with foil.
Roast for 7–8 hours, until the meat is so tender it shreds easily when pulled with two forks.
Remove from oven and let rest for 10 minutes, then shred the meat into bite-sized pieces, discarding the bone and most of the skin (save a bit of crispy skin to mix back in if you like).
Serve warm with the pan juices spooned over.

notes: Kalua pork keeps well in the fridge for 4 days, and freezes for up to 3 months. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
Serve with rice, cabbage slaw and gravy for a real plate lunch, or use it for musubi.
The longer you cook it, the more tender it gets, even 8 or 9 hours won't hurt.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Smørrebrød med roastbeef og remoulade
summary: Classic Danish open sandwich with roast beef, sharp remoulade, crispy onions and pickled cucumber on dark rye.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g good-quality roast beef, thinly sliced

steps.text: Make the remoulade: whisk together mayonnaise, Dijon mustard and wholegrain mustard until smooth. Fold in the capers and pickled gherkin. Add lemon juice and season with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust the mustard or lemon if needed.
Lightly butter each slice of bread, spreading it all the way to the edges.
Lay the roast beef slices on top of the butter in a slightly overlapping layer, until the bread is fully covered and the beef is soft and draped.
Spoon remoulade generously over the beef.
Top with pickled cucumber slices and a handful of crispy fried onions.
Garnish with a small sprig of fresh parsley and serve immediately.

notes: Make the remoulade up to 3 days ahead and keep it in the fridge.
Use really good-quality roast beef sliced thin from the deli counter, it makes all the difference.
Assemble the smørrebrød just before serving so the bread stays crisp and the onions don't soften too much.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Bap with Gochujang Butter
summary: Rice with a Korean chilli-butter scramble and a fried egg.

steps.text: Mix the butter and gochujang together in a small bowl until combined.
Heat a small non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Crack the egg into the pan and fry until the white is set and the yolk is still runny, about 2–3 minutes.
While the egg cooks, put the rice in a serving bowl.
Transfer the fried egg to a plate and set aside.
Return the frying pan to medium heat. Add the gochujang butter and sesame oil, stirring until the butter melts and the mixture is warm, about 1 minute.
Pour the gochujang butter over the rice and stir through. Top with the fried egg and scatter the spring onion over the top.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed, then serve straight away.

notes: Make the gochujang butter ahead and keep it in a pot in the fridge; it'll come together faster in the morning.
Use leftover rice from the night before, or make a quick batch while you wait for the egg to fry.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Sago Pudding
summary: Creamy sago with cinnamon, cardamom and rose water, comfort in a bowl.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large saucepan. Add the sago slowly, stirring constantly to prevent lumps from forming. Cook, stirring often, until the sago is translucent and tender, about 12 minutes.
Add the milk, caster sugar, cinnamon stick and crushed cardamom pods. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer until the sugar has dissolved and the milk is fragrant.
Cook, stirring occasionally, until the pudding thickens slightly and the sago pearls are completely soft, about 5 minutes. The mixture should be creamy but not stiff.
Remove from the heat and stir through the rose water. Taste and add a pinch of salt to balance the sweetness. Discard the cinnamon stick.
Divide among bowls while still warm and dust lightly with ground cinnamon. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: This pudding can be made a few hours ahead and gently reheated, or served at room temperature.
Use good-quality rose water, it should smell fragrant but not perfumy. Add it slowly and taste as you go.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Arròs Negre
summary: Catalan black rice with squid ink, fresh squid and seafood on a slow sofregit base.

items.raw: 400 g tinned tomatoes, sieved or blended smooth
Salt and black pepper, to taste
350 g short-grain rice (bomba or paella rice preferred)
300 g fresh squid, cleaned and cut into rings
2 sachets squid ink (4 g total, or fresh ink from fishmonger)
items.note: 4 g total, or fresh ink from fishmonger

items.raw: 750 ml seafood stock (or fish stock), warmed

steps.text: In your rice pan or large shallow casserole over medium heat, warm the olive oil. Add the chopped onions and cook very slowly, stirring often, until completely soft and lightly golden, this is the sofregit, and it should take 12 to 15 minutes. Do not rush it; this is where the flavour lives.
Add the tinned tomatoes to the sofregit and stir well. Cook for another 5 to 8 minutes, until the sauce thickens slightly and the raw tomato taste disappears. Season with salt and pepper.
Stir in the garlic and chilli (if using), and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes, coating each grain with the sofregit and oil.

Dissolve the squid ink sachets in the warm stock until the stock is jet black, then pour the stock gradually into the rice, stirring occasionally. Bring to a simmer until bubbles break across the surface.
Cook the rice uncovered at a gentle simmer for about 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is almost tender and the liquid has been mostly absorbed.

Scatter the squid rings and mussels across the top of the rice. Do not stir them in. Continue cooking for 5 to 7 minutes, until the squid is just cooked through, the mussel shells have opened (discard any that don't), and the rice is tender with a slight bite. The bottom should form a thin, crispy layer (called socarrat).
Remove from heat, cover loosely with foil, and rest for 3 minutes. Scatter fresh parsley over the top and serve at the table in the pan.

notes: Make the sofregit ahead: cook the onions and tomatoes up to an hour before, then reheat gently before adding the rice.
Fresh squid ink from the fishmonger can replace the sachets, ask for 2 sachets' worth (about 4 g). It will be fresher and give a rounder flavour.
Arròs negre reheats poorly, so cook it fresh and serve at once, still warm from the pan.

Food safety: Cook fish until it turns opaque and flakes easily, about 63°C in the thickest part. Cook mussels and clams only if they are alive and tightly closed (or close when tapped), and throw out any that stay shut after cooking. Cook squid, octopus and scallops until opaque and just firm, and keep seafood chilled until you cook it. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Banga Soup
summary: Palm nut soup with stockfish and crayfish, rich and deeply savoury.

items.raw: 1 kg fresh palm nuts, husked and cleaned
4 scotch bonnet chillies, whole (optional, for heat)

steps.text: Pound the palm nuts in a large bowl with 2 litres of hot water (not boiling), working in batches. Press through a fine sieve or colander lined with muslin cloth, squeezing gently to extract all the cream. Reserve this golden liquid and discard the fibre.

In a large pot, bring 1 litre of water to the boil. Add the stockfish, one halved onion, and a pinch of salt. Simmer for 20 minutes, then remove the stockfish and set aside to cool. Strain the cooking liquid and reserve it (discard the onion).
Once the stockfish is cool enough to handle, remove the meat from the bones and break into chunks. Discard the bones.
Pour the palm nut cream into the pot over medium heat. Stir constantly for 3–4 minutes until it thickens slightly and the oil begins to separate on top, this is how you know it's ready.

Add the reserved stockfish cooking liquid, the stockfish meat, dried crayfish, remaining halved onion, and the scotch bonnet chillies if using. Stir well and simmer gently for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Stir in the ground crayfish, salt, and black pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning. Simmer for another 10 minutes, then remove from heat. Remove the onion halves and whole chillies before serving.
Serve hot with boiled white rice, gari, or fufu.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently, the flavours deepen overnight.
If you can't find fresh palm nuts, use tinned palm cream (about 800 ml), though fresh is far superior. Skip the pounding and straining; just heat the tinned cream gently and follow from step 3.
Stockfish is essential, dried, smoked whole fish. Don't substitute with stock cubes or powder, you'll lose the soul of the soup.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Chikuwa Don
summary: Bowl of rice topped with simmered fish cake and egg, quick bento favourite.

steps.text: Combine dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar in a small saucepan or shallow pan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat until the sugar has dissolved and small bubbles appear at the edges.
Add the sliced chikuwa and simmer for 2 minutes until heated through.
Lightly beat the eggs in a bowl. Pour into the simmering broth in a thin stream, stirring gently until the egg is just set but still soft, about 1 minute.
Divide the cooked rice between two bowls. Spoon the chikuwa, egg and sauce over the top. Garnish with spring onion if using, and serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: Cook the rice and prepare the chikuwa mixture up to 4 hours ahead. Reheat gently and pour over fresh rice.
Chikuwa keeps in the fridge for up to a week, so this is perfect for bento prep.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Kik Alicha
summary: Mild yellow split pea wat with ginger and turmeric, Ethiopian fasting-day comfort food.

steps.text: Heat the niter kibbeh in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger and cook, stirring, for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the turmeric and cardamom, and cook for 1 minute to bloom the spices.

Add the rinsed split peas and water. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the peas break down and the wat thickens, about 30 minutes. The peas should be completely soft and the sauce creamy.
Season with salt to taste. If the wat is too thick, add a splash more water. Serve warm with injera.

notes: Make this on fasting days (Wednesday and Friday for the Ethiopian Orthodox calendar). It's just as good made with neutral oil instead of niter kibbeh if you're fasting from animal products.
Kik alicha keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen the sauce.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Jianbing
summary: Crispy crepe with egg, spring onions and wonton, Northern China's street breakfast.

steps.text: Mix plain flour and salt in a bowl. Slowly add water, stirring until smooth. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.
While the batter rests, break the wonton wrappers into rough pieces and fry in a small pan with a little oil until crispy and golden, about 2 minutes. Set aside.
Heat a large non-stick pan or crepe pan over high heat. It should be very hot, test with a drop of water; it should sizzle and evaporate immediately.
Pour 120 ml of batter into the centre of the pan and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so the batter spreads into a thin, even circle about 20 cm across. Work quickly.
Let the batter cook for about 30 seconds until the bottom is set and starts to turn light golden. Crack an egg onto one half of the crepe, then use a spatula to break the yolk and spread it evenly.
Scatter half the chopped spring onion and half the crispy wonton pieces over the egg. Fold the other half of the crepe over to enclose the filling, pressing gently.
Cook for another 30 seconds until the egg is set, then slide onto a plate. Serve immediately with sweet chilli sauce and soy sauce for dipping.
Repeat with the remaining batter, egg, spring onion and wonton to make a second jianbing.

notes: The batter can be made the night before and stored in the fridge, it actually develops better flavour overnight.
Wonton wrappers crisp up quickly, so fry them just before you start making the crepes.
A non-stick or well-seasoned crepe pan is essential. The pan must be hot enough that the batter sets instantly, or you'll struggle to spread it.

title: Za'atar Bread
summary: Warm Palestinian flatbread brushed with olive oil and za'atar spice mix.

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine flour and salt. Make a well in the centre and pour in the warm water. Mix with your hand until a shaggy dough forms, then knead for 5 minutes until smooth and slightly elastic.
Divide dough into 4 balls. Cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes while you set up to cook.
Toast the za'atar in a dry frying pan over medium heat for about 30 seconds, stirring constantly, until fragrant. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.

Place the same frying pan over medium heat. Working with one ball at a time, flatten the dough with your hands into a rough oval about 5 mm thick. Cook for about 1.5 to 2 minutes, until it puffs slightly and the bottom is pale golden.
Flip and cook the other side for another 1 to 1.5 minutes. The bread should be flexible, not crispy. Transfer to a plate.
While warm, brush the bread with olive oil on both sides, then sprinkle generously with the toasted za'atar and a pinch of salt. Repeat with remaining dough balls and serve warm.

notes: Make the dough ahead: prepare through step 2, cover, and refrigerate overnight. Bring to room temperature before cooking.
Za'atar is a Palestinian blend of thyme, sumac and sesame. Look for it in Middle Eastern grocers or make your own by mixing 1 tbsp dried thyme, 1 tbsp sumac and 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds.

title: Buniga ni Lolo
summary: Fijian eggplant braised in coconut milk with spices, tender and rich.

items.raw: 3 medium eggplants, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cumin, coriander and turmeric, and cook for 1 minute to release the spices.
Add the eggplant chunks and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until gentle bubbles appear and the sauce is slightly thickened. Add the chopped chillies and stir well.
Reduce heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 20 minutes until the eggplant is very tender. Stir occasionally.
Taste and add salt as needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Serve with roti, dhal puri or rice.
You can add 2 or 3 curry leaves and a sprig of fresh coriander in the last 5 minutes of cooking if you have them.

title: Bánh Nậm
summary: Folded rice cakes with pork and shrimp filling, a Central Vietnamese specialty.

items.raw: Banana leaves, cut into 15 cm squares (about 8 pieces), or plastic wrap
items.prep: cut into 15 cm squares, or plastic wrap

items.raw: Pickled mixed vegetables (pickled daikon and carrot, pickled onion, or pickled mustard greens)
items.note: pickled daikon and carrot, pickled onion, or pickled mustard greens

steps.text: Make the rice cake batter: Mix rice flour and salt. Gradually add water, stirring until smooth. The batter should be thin and pourable, like crepe batter. Let it rest 10 minutes.

Make the filling: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add shallots and garlic, cook stirring for 2 minutes until fragrant. Add pork mince, breaking it up as it cooks. After 5 minutes, add chopped prawn, fish sauce and black pepper. Cook, stirring, for another 3 minutes until the prawn is just cooked through. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside to cool slightly.
Prepare banana leaves or plastic: If using banana leaves, blanch them briefly in hot water to soften, then lay flat to cool. If using plastic wrap, cut into squares and lay flat.

Cook the rice cakes: Lightly oil a non-stick frying pan (about 20 cm) and heat over medium-high heat. Pour about 60 ml of batter into the pan, tilting to spread it into a thin, roughly square sheet about 3 mm thick. Cook for about 1 minute until the edges lift and the top is just set but still pliable. Slide onto a banana leaf or plastic, cooked side up. Repeat to make 8 cakes.

Fill and fold: While still warm, place about 2 tbsp of cooled filling in the centre of each rice cake. Fold one corner over the filling, then the next corner, then the next, creating an envelope. The final corner should tuck under. The rice cake should be soft enough to fold without cracking.
