Set the bánh nậm: Let each folded cake sit on its banana leaf or plastic for a few minutes to firm up slightly. They can be eaten warm or at room temperature.

Serve: Arrange bánh nậm on a platter with pickled vegetables and fresh herbs on the side. Make a simple dipping sauce by stirring a small amount of fish sauce into water (about 1 part fish sauce to 3 parts water). Serve with rice paper crisps if you like extra crunch.

notes: Make the rice cakes up to 2 hours ahead and keep them at room temperature, covered with a damp cloth. Assemble and fold just before serving so they stay pliable.
If you can't find banana leaves, plastic wrap works fine, or serve the bánh nậm on a plate with lettuce underneath instead.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Slow-Roasted Tomatoes and Onions with Oregano
summary: Slow-roasted tomatoes and onions collapse into soft, silky jam with olive oil and oregano.

items.raw: 4 brown onions, sliced into thick rings

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Arrange the tomato halves cut-side up in a large baking dish, nestling the onion rings between and around them.
Drizzle generously with olive oil and scatter the dried oregano over everything. Season with salt and pepper.
Roast, uncovered, for 90 minutes, stirring gently halfway through. The tomatoes should collapse and release their liquid, and the onions should soften and begin to caramelize at the edges.
The gemista is ready when the tomatoes have broken down completely and the liquid has reduced to a thick, jammy consistency. Serve warm with crusty bread.

notes: Serve warm or at room temperature with crusty bread for scooping.
Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day.
The notebook's version with dried tomatoes works too, reduce the roasting time to about 45 minutes if using them.

title: Lentil Kibbeh
summary: Bulgur and red lentil shells stuffed with spiced lentil filling, baked instead of fried.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: For the filling, heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Add the cumin, coriander and allspice, stirring until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the brown lentils and cook, stirring occasionally, until just tender and any liquid has been absorbed, about 20 minutes. Stir through the pine nuts, then season to taste. Set aside to cool.

For the shells, heat the olive oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the brown onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the cumin, coriander, cinnamon and cayenne, stirring until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the red lentils and cook, stirring often, for 2 minutes. Pour in the vegetable stock and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the lentils are completely broken down and the mixture is thick and creamy, about 15 minutes. Stir through the bulgur until fully incorporated, then remove from the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes. Season to taste.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Once the shell mixture is cool enough to handle, wet your hands lightly and form a spoonful of the mixture into an oblong shell shape. Make an indentation in the centre with your thumb, fill with about a teaspoon of the cooled lentil filling, then press the opening closed and shape into an oval or leaf. Repeat with the remaining mixture.

Lightly oil a baking tray and arrange the kibbeh on it in a single layer. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until the kibbeh are firm and lightly golden on the outside. Serve warm with fresh lemon and a simple salad.

notes: The kibbeh can be assembled up to 4 hours ahead, covered and chilled. Bake just before serving.
Serve with tahini sauce, hummus, or a squeeze of fresh lemon and a simple salad of tomato, cucumber and parsley.

title: Saganaki
summary: Fried halloumi cheese that squeaks between your teeth, golden and crispy with lemon.

items.raw: 250 g halloumi, cut into 8 mm slices

steps.text: Heat a shallow pan over medium-high heat. Pour in enough oil so it's about 5 mm deep, then get it really hot, it should shimmer and just start to smoke.
Dust the halloumi slices lightly in flour on both sides, shaking off any excess.
When the oil's smoking, carefully lay the halloumi slices into the pan. You should hear them sizzle immediately. Don't move them.
Cook for about 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden. Flip and cook the other side for another 2 minutes until it's the same colour. It should squeak when you bite into it.
Transfer to a plate, season with salt, and serve straight away with lemon wedges on the side. Squeeze lemon over each piece and eat it hot.

notes: Halloumi must be proper Cyprus halloumi, soft halloumi will melt and won't squeak. Find it at the deli counter or with the international cheeses.
Eat it straight from the pan while it's still hot and squeaky. Once it cools, it toughens up.
This works as an appetiser before a big feed, or as a quick snack with cold beer on a Saturday arvo.

title: Shami Kebab
summary: Spiced ground meat and lentil kebabs, pan-fried until golden and crispy.

steps.text: Boil the lentils in 400 ml water with a pinch of salt until very soft and the water is absorbed, about 20 minutes. Cool completely.
Mix the cooked lentils, beef mince, chopped onion, garlic, ginger garlic paste, green chillies, coriander and mint in a large bowl. Add the cumin, coriander, garam masala, turmeric, salt and pepper.
Beat the egg lightly and mix it into the meat mixture until well combined. Cover and refrigerate for at least 15 minutes (this helps the mixture hold together).
Wet your hands lightly with water. Divide the mixture into 8 portions and shape each into a tight oval patty about 7 cm long and 3 cm thick.

Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. When the oil is hot, carefully place 4 kebabs in the pan. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes on the first side until golden and crispy, then flip and fry the other side for another 5 to 6 minutes until cooked through.
Transfer the cooked kebabs to a plate lined with paper towel. Repeat with the remaining 4 kebabs, adding another tablespoon of oil if needed.
Serve hot with mint chutney, sliced raw onion and lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead, cover and refrigerate until ready to fry.
For extra flavour, add 1 tbsp of tamarind paste to the mixture before shaping.
These freeze well raw: freeze shaped kebabs on a tray, then transfer to a container. Fry from frozen, allowing an extra 2 to 3 minutes per side.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Huîtres gratinées au beurre et persil
summary: Oysters baked with herb butter and crispy breadcrumb topping

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 200°C. Shuck the oysters, keeping them in their bottom shell and reserving any liquid.
Mix the softened butter with the parsley, garlic, salt and pepper until well combined.
Arrange the oysters in their shells on a baking tray. Top each with about 1 tsp of herb butter.
Sprinkle the breadcrumbs evenly over each oyster, pressing gently so they stick to the butter.
Bake for 8 minutes, until the breadcrumbs are golden and the butter is bubbling around the edges.
Serve at once, with lemon wedges on the side.

notes: The oysters must be eaten as soon as they come out of the oven, while the butter is still foaming.
If shucking oysters yourself, chill them in the freezer for 15 minutes first, they open more easily.
You can make the herb butter a few hours ahead and chill it, then scoop it on to the oysters just before baking.

title: Crispy Tofu Rice Paper Rolls with Chilli Dipping Sauce
summary: Fresh rice paper rolls with fried tofu, herbs and quick sweet chilli sauce.

steps.text: Cut the pressed tofu into 16 rectangular fingers, about 1 cm thick. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Once hot, fry the tofu in two batches for 2–3 minutes each side, until golden and crispy. Set aside on paper towel.
While the tofu cools, make the dipping sauce by stirring together the sweet chilli sauce, rice vinegar, soy sauce and sesame oil in a small bowl. Stir in the sliced chilli if using.
Fill a shallow bowl with warm water. Dip one rice paper into the water for 2–3 seconds until just pliable, then lay it flat on a clean board.

Arrange 2 tofu fingers down the centre of the paper, then top with a small handful of salad leaves, a few mint and coriander leaves, and some cucumber and carrot matchsticks. Add a piece of spring onion.
Fold the bottom edge of the rice paper up and over the filling, fold in the sides, then roll forward tightly until sealed.
Place seam-side down on a plate and repeat with the remaining rice papers and filling.
Serve the rolls immediately with the chilli dipping sauce on the side.

notes: Press the tofu overnight or for at least 2 hours before cooking so it fries crispy and stays that way. You can make the filling components ahead and assemble the rolls right before serving.
Swap the herbs for whatever's fresh, Thai basil works beautifully, or try rocket for something peppery.

title: Squid and Chilli
summary: Quick-fried squid with local chilli, garlic and lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Score the squid tubes in a fine crosshatch, cutting about halfway through the flesh. Pat dry with paper towel and cut into bite-sized pieces (about 4 cm square).
Place a large frying pan or wok over high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the olive oil, then immediately add the squid pieces, chilli and garlic. Stir constantly for about 2 minutes, the squid will curl and become opaque.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, then squeeze lemon juice over and toss through.
Serve immediately, scattered with fresh parsley if you like, with extra lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Don't overcrowd the pan, if you're cooking for more than 4, cook in two batches so the squid fries rather than steams.
Squid cooks fast: longer than 3–4 minutes and it toughens. In and out.
Serve with crusty bread to mop up the pan juices.
Food safety: Cook squid, octopus and scallops until opaque and just firm, and keep seafood chilled until you cook it.

title: Tortelloni di Ricotta e Spinaci
summary: Hand-folded ricotta and spinach pasta with brown butter and sage.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pasta dough: tip flour into a mound on a work surface, make a well in the centre, crack in eggs, add oil and a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Wrap and rest 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the filling: mix ricotta, spinach, parmesan, egg yolk and garlic. Season generously with salt, pepper and nutmeg, taste it, it should be well-seasoned.
Dust your work surface. Roll the dough to the thickness of a coin (about 1 mm). Using a 7 cm round cutter, stamp out circles.

Place a small spoonful of filling (about ½ tsp) on one half of each circle. Fold in half, press the edges to seal, then fold the corners up and press them together to make a purse shape. Place on a floured tray as you go.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Melt the butter in a separate pan over medium heat until it turns golden and smells nutty, 5 minutes. Add the sage leaves.

Drop the agnolotti into the boiling water. They'll sink, then bob to the surface after 2–3 minutes. Cook for another 2 minutes, then remove with a slotted spoon and add to the brown butter. Toss gently.
Divide among bowls. Add a pinch of salt and grate parmesan over the top.

notes: Make the pasta and filling up to 2 hours ahead; keep the cut agnolotti on a tray in the fridge, uncovered, until you cook them.
If your filling is too wet, the agnolotti will split. If the ricotta is very creamy, drain it in a sieve lined with kitchen paper for 10 minutes first.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

title: Mee Goreng Mamak
summary: Spicy stir-fried noodles with egg and prawns, Malaysian street food done at home.

items.raw: 250 g fresh egg noodles (or cooked noodles)
2 spring onion, cut into 3 cm lengths
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Blend or pound the garlic, chillies, sambal oelek, tomato paste and turmeric into a rough paste.
Heat the oil in your best pan over medium-high heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring, until fragrant and the oil starts to separate from the paste, about 2 minutes.
Add the prawns and stir-fry for 2 minutes until they just start to turn pink.
Push everything to the side. Crack the eggs into the cleared space and let them sit for 30 seconds, then scramble them lightly and mix with the prawns and paste.
Add the noodles and break them up as you stir-fry, coating them with the paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the soy sauce and kecap manis, toss until the noodles are coated and heated through, about 1 minute.
Remove from heat. Stir through the lime juice, bean sprouts and spring onion. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.
Serve hot with lime wedges and coriander, if using.

notes: Use fresh egg noodles from the fridge section if you can, they won't clump. No fresh? Cooked noodles work fine; just break them up as you add them.
The paste can be made 30 minutes ahead and kept in a bowl.
Push for medium heat, you want the paste to fry properly but the noodles not to burn on the bottom.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Curry Duck
summary: Tender duck slow-cooked in fragrant spiced curry, a Trinidadian special occasion dish.

items.raw: 1 whole duck (about 2 kg), cut into 8 pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Dry-roast the coriander and cumin seeds in a small pan over medium heat, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Grind to a fine powder and set aside. Mix the ground roasted spices with the crushed garlic and grated ginger to form a paste.

Pat the duck pieces dry with paper towel. Season with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the duck on all sides, about 3 minutes per side. Set aside.

In the same pot, add the diced onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the curry powder and tomato paste, stirring constantly, for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the spice-garlic-ginger paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes.

Return the duck to the pot. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock. Add the whole green chillies and curry leaves. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low, cover, and cook gently for 1½ hours, or until the duck is very tender and the meat pulls easily from the bone.

Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. If the sauce is too thin, uncover and simmer for a further 10 minutes to reduce. Serve the curry duck hot with warm roti, using the bread to soak up the rich spiced sauce.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently on the stove; the flavours deepen overnight.
Whole green chillies stay mild if you don't break them open; remove them before serving if you prefer no heat.
Duck makes this special, but chicken thighs work if duck is hard to find. Reduce the cook time to 45 minutes.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Tomato Rice with Eggs
summary: Fried rice with tomato and chilli, topped with crispy eggs.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, if using, and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the rice, breaking up any clumps, and cook for 3 minutes, stirring often, until the rice is heated through and beginning to catch on the pan.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes and their juice. Stir well, then cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomato is absorbed and the rice is heated through. Season with salt and pepper.

Push the rice to the sides of the pan, creating a small space in the centre. Crack both eggs into the space, then cover the pan with a lid or foil. Cook for 2–3 minutes until the eggs are cooked to your liking (the whites should be set but the yolks still soft).
Remove from the heat and scatter with fresh coriander, if using. Divide between two bowls and serve.

notes: Make sure your rice is cooled first, this stops it from becoming mushy. Leftover rice from yesterday works perfectly.
If you don't have tinned tomatoes, use 150 g of fresh tomato, chopped, or 2 tbsp tomato paste mixed with 2 tbsp water.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Cavolfiore Affogato
summary: Cauliflower braised in tomato and garlic until it falls apart, a southern Italian vegetable dish.

items.raw: 1 medium cauliflower, about 800 g, cut into florets
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 3 minutes.
Add the cauliflower florets and stir to coat in the oil and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and dried oregano. Stir well to combine. Season with salt and pepper.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover and braise for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cauliflower is very tender and beginning to break down. The sauce should be thick and fragrant.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like, with good bread to soak up the sauce.

notes: Best served warm with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.
Keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's too thick.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Perlou
summary: One-pot Low Country rice with chicken and sausage, simmered in savory broth.

items.raw: 400 g good-quality pork sausage, cut into 2 cm pieces
600 g chicken thigh, cut into 4 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large cast iron pan over medium-high heat. Brown the sausage pieces until golden on all sides, about 5 minutes, then remove and set aside on a plate.
Add the chicken pieces to the pan and brown until golden, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside with the sausage.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the rice to the pan and stir constantly for 2 minutes, letting the grains toast lightly in the oil.
Pour in the chicken stock and stir well, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Return the sausage and chicken to the pan, along with any juices. Add the salt and pepper.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid or foil, and cook for 25 to 30 minutes, until the rice is tender and has absorbed all the broth. Stir once halfway through cooking.
Remove from the heat and let rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, top with fresh parsley if you like, and serve straight from the pan.

notes: Use bone-in chicken thighs if you can find them, they add more flavour to the broth as everything cooks.
This keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

Food safety: Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches 75°C and the juices run clear, with no pink meat near the bone. Cook mince, sausages, meatballs and liver right through to 75°C, with no pink in the centre.

title: Naam Tok Gai
summary: Grilled chicken with lime dressing, fish sauce, fresh herbs and crispy rice powder.

steps.text: Toast the jasmine rice in a dry frying pan over medium heat, shaking often, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 3–4 minutes. Let it cool, then pound it in a mortar until it's crumbly with some fine powder, not flour-fine, but grainy.

Pat the chicken dry and brush lightly with oil. Heat a chargrill or barbecue to high, then grill the chicken, turning once, until cooked through (75°C inside), about 8–10 minutes. Let it rest for 2 minutes, then slice into bite-sized pieces.
Whisk the lime juice, fish sauce and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Put the warm chicken in a large bowl with the dressing and toss well. Add the toasted rice powder, green chilli, coriander, mint and spring onions, and toss again.
Taste and add salt or a squeeze more lime juice if you need it. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The toasted rice powder is the heart of this dish, make it fresh each time you cook. It won't keep.
Naam tok is best eaten warm, but it's fine at room temperature too. Leftovers don't hold up overnight.
Food safety: Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches 75°C and the juices run clear, with no pink meat near the bone.

title: Grilled Lapu-Lapu with Vinegar Dip
summary: Whole reef grouper char-grilled and served with a sharp vinegar, chilli and garlic dip.

items.raw: 1 whole grouper (1–1.2 kg), scaled and gutted
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the vinegar dip: combine vinegar, garlic, chilli and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the flavours come together.

Pat the grouper dry inside and out. Make three shallow scores across each side of the fish – this helps it cook through and caramelises the skin. Brush lightly with oil and season generously with salt and pepper, inside the cavity and on both sides.
Heat a large char-grill or grill plate to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Oil the grates well.

Place the grouper on the grill and cook without moving it for 8–10 minutes, until the skin is charred and crisp and releases easily from the grate. Flip carefully and cook the other side for 8–10 minutes, until the flesh near the backbone is opaque and cooked through (check by inserting a knife at the thickest point).
Transfer to a warm plate, squeeze lime over it and serve at the table with the vinegar dip on the side for each person to help themselves.

notes: Best cooked and eaten the same day the fish is caught or bought. The fresher the grouper, the sweeter the flesh.
If you don't have a char-grill, use a heavy-bottomed frying pan over high heat, or cook the fish wrapped in foil in a hot oven at 200°C for about 20 minutes.
The vinegar dip keeps for a few days in a jar in the fridge – use it with other grilled fish or seafood.

title: Snags and Onion Gravy
summary: Quality sausages with caramelised onion gravy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy pan or cast-iron frying pan over medium-high heat. Brown the sausages all over until golden, about 8 minutes. Set aside.

In the same pan, add the sliced onions and reduce heat to medium-low. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions are soft and deep golden brown, about 20 minutes. Be patient, this is where the flavour comes from.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the beef stock and worcestershire sauce. Return the sausages to the pan.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes until the sausages are cooked through and the gravy has thickened slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Serve the snags on a plate with the onion gravy spooned over.

notes: Mash or mashed potato on the side soaks up the gravy beautifully.
Use a good butcher's sausage, it makes all the difference.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Cassava Cake
summary: Grated cassava baked with coconut milk and sugar, dense and chewy.

items.raw: 1 kg cassava, peeled and finely grated

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line a 20 cm × 30 cm baking tin with baking paper.
Squeeze the grated cassava firmly over a bowl to remove excess moisture, this is important for the right texture. Transfer to a large bowl.
Add the coconut milk, caster sugar, vanilla extract and salt. Stir well until the sugar is dissolved and everything is combined.
Pour into the prepared tin, spreading evenly.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until the top is golden and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack to cool completely. Cut into squares to serve.

notes: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or refrigerate for up to a week.
This cake is best made a day ahead, the flavour deepens and the texture becomes even better.
Don't skip squeezing out the moisture from the cassava; it makes all the difference to how the cake sets.

title: Barramundi with Thai Basil and Chilli
summary: Pan-fried local barramundi finished with fragrant holy basil and fresh bird's eye chilli.

items.raw: 4 barramundi fillet, 150–180 g each, skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste
2 birds-eye-chilli, sliced into rings (seeds removed for less heat, optional)
1 cup fresh Thai basil leaves (or 3/4 cup if using regular basil)
items.note: or 3/4 cup if using regular basil

items.raw: 1 lime, cut into wedges, to serve

steps.text: Pat the barramundi dry with paper towel. Season skin side lightly with salt and pepper.
Heat 1 tbsp of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers, place the barramundi skin side down. Cook for 4–5 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp and golden.
Flip the fillets gently and cook for a further 2–3 minutes, until the flesh is just cooked through (it should flake easily but still be moist inside). Transfer to a warm plate.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the remaining oil to the same pan, then add the garlic and sliced chilli. Cook, stirring gently, for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Tear in the fresh basil, pour the fish sauce over it, and toss through for about 10 seconds until the basil just wilts.
Spoon the basil and chilli mixture over the barramundi and serve at once with lime wedges on the side.

notes: Barramundi is best when fresh and cooked simply. If you can't find barramundi, use any firm white fish fillet like snapper or bream.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice and a quick salad of cucumber and lime to cut through the richness.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Lumpia Goreng
summary: Crispy fried spring rolls stuffed with cabbage and tempeh.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add tempeh and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 minutes until it starts to brown.
Add cabbage and cook, stirring, until soft and any liquid has evaporated, about 5 minutes. Season with soy sauce, pepper and salt. Transfer to a plate and cool for 10 minutes.
Lay a lumpia wrapper on a clean surface with one corner pointing towards you. Place 1 tbsp of filling in the centre.

Fold the bottom corner up over the filling, then fold in the left and right corners. Roll tightly away from you, then wet the top corner with water and seal. Place seam-side down on a plate. Repeat with remaining wrappers and filling.
Heat 1 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C. Working in batches, fry lumpia for 2 to 3 minutes on each side until golden and crispy. Drain on paper towel and serve hot.

title: Horenso No Ohitashi
summary: Blanched spinach dressed in cold dashi, bonito and soy, the quiet vegetable side that never fails.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the spinach, stirring gently, until tender and wilted, about 2 minutes. Drain in a colander.
Gather the spinach into a ball and gently squeeze out excess water with your hands. Do this carefully, the leaves should stay tender. Set aside to cool.
Combine the dashi, soy sauce and mirin in a bowl. Chill in the refrigerator until cold.
Once the spinach has cooled, cut it into 4 cm lengths and arrange in a serving bowl or on a plate.
Pour the cold dashi dressing over the spinach just before serving, or let each person pour their own at the table. Top with bonito flakes.
Serve immediately, chilled.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dashi dressing the night before and keep chilled.
The spinach must be cooled completely before dressing, or the dashi will warm and lose its clean taste.
Serve in shallow bowls if you have them, obanzai looks best on good ceramics.

title: Gat Kimchi
summary: Mustard leaf kimchi with gentle bite and deep, funky fermented flavour.

items.raw: 800 g mustard greens (gat), leaves and stems separated
2 spring onions, chopped into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Make the paste: whisk glutinous rice flour, water and sugar in a saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly, until thickened and translucent, about 3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the garlic, ginger, gochugaru and fish sauce. Set aside to cool slightly.
Prepare the gat: cut the stems into 5 cm lengths. Leave the leaves whole or tear into 10 cm pieces if very large. Rinse well under cold water.

Salt the gat: layer the stems and leaves in a large bowl, sprinkling 2 tbsp of salt evenly as you go. Let sit for 15 minutes, then massage gently with your hands, turning the leaves over to coat all sides. The gat will soften and release liquid, this is correct. Drain off most of the liquid.

Season: add the cooled paste to the salted gat along with the spring onions and sesame seeds. Using clean hands, toss and massage everything together for 2 minutes so every leaf is coated. Taste a small piece: it should taste pleasantly salty now, but not salty enough to eat as is, the flavour will develop as it ferments.

Pack: transfer the gat kimchi into a clean glass jar, pressing down so the vegetables are submerged under their own liquid. Leave a 5 cm gap at the top. If there isn't enough liquid to cover, sprinkle the remaining 1 tbsp salt over the top and leave for 10 minutes to release more brine.

Ferment: seal the jar loosely (not airtight) and leave at cool room temperature or in the cold part of your kitchen for 3 days. After day 1, open the lid to let gas escape. By day 3, it will have a gentle fizz and a deep, funky flavour. Taste it, when it suits you, seal it tightly and refrigerate. It will keep for up to 3 weeks.

notes: Make sure your jar is very clean and dry before packing. A sterilised jam jar works perfectly.
The 3-day fermentation at cool room temperature is ideal. In summer, ferment in the coldest part of your fridge and add 1–2 days.
Once fermented and refrigerated, open the jar every few days to release gas, or it will build pressure.

title: Masgouf
summary: Grilled whole fish with spiced tamarind marinade, the Baghdad way.

items.raw: 2 whole barramundi (or carp), about 600 g each, cleaned and gutted
items.prep: about 600 g each, cleaned and gutted

steps.text: Make the marinade: whisk together pomegranate molasses, tamarind paste, oil, garlic, cumin, coriander, Aleppo pepper and salt in a small bowl.
Prepare the fish: lay each fish on a cutting board and, using a sharp knife, cut down the spine from head to tail. Gently press the fish open so it lies flat like a butterfly, skin side down.
Rub the marinade all over the fish, inside and out, making sure to coat the flesh well. Let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a large heavy-based pan or cast iron frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully lay the fish skin side up in the pan.

Cook for 6–7 minutes without moving, until the skin is golden and crispy. Gently flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until the flesh is opaque and cooked through (the flesh should flake easily when pressed with a fork).
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh parsley scattered over.

notes: If charcoal is available, this is traditionally cooked over open flame. Adjust your grill or pan to get good colour without burning the delicate flesh.
Carp is the traditional Baghdad fish, but barramundi or any firm white fish works well. Ask your fishmonger to clean and gut the fish for you if you prefer.

title: Beef and Burdock Don
summary: Thinly sliced beef cooked down with earthy burdock root, quick weeknight donburi

items.raw: 400 g beef sirloin (or rump), thinly sliced
300 g burdock, scrubbed and cut into matchsticks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok over high heat. Cook the beef in batches until browned on the outside, about 2 minutes per batch. Set aside.
Add the burdock and onion to the same pan. Stir-fry for 2 minutes until the onion softens slightly.

Return the beef to the pan. Add the soy sauce, mirin, sugar and water. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until the burdock is tender and the sauce has reduced by half, about 5 minutes.
Divide the hot steamed rice among bowls. Spoon the beef and burdock mixture over the top and scatter with spring onions. Serve straight away.

notes: Shave the burdock on a mandoline or with a vegetable peeler to keep the pieces thin and cook evenly.
You can make this with chicken thigh or thinly sliced pork instead of beef, same cooking time.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Mashed Potatoes with Crispy Onions and Dill
summary: Buttery mashed potatoes loaded with fried onions and fresh dill, a side dish that becomes dinner when you're lazy.

items.raw: 900 g waxy potatoes, peeled and halved
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add potatoes and cook until completely tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well in a colander.

While potatoes cook, heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add onions and cook, stirring occasionally, until they're golden and crispy, about 12 minutes. Season with salt and transfer to a paper towel.

Mash warm potatoes with butter and milk until creamy but still with a little texture. Fold in most of the crispy onions and all the dill, reserving some onions for the top. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Transfer to a serving bowl and top with reserved crispy onions. Eat immediately.

title: Pipi Soup
summary: Creamy broth with pipis, kumara and fresh herbs from the kai moana.

items.raw: 400 g kumara (sweet potato), peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 lemon, cut into wedges, to serve

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for another minute until it smells good. Stir in the kumara and cook for 2 minutes to warm it through.
Pour in the stock and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until the kumara is tender, about 12 minutes.
Add the pipis and the cream, stirring gently. Cover and simmer until all the pipi shells have opened, about 5 to 8 minutes. Discard any that don't open.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Scatter the spring onion and coriander over the top and serve hot with lemon wedges.
Squeeze the lemon over the soup before eating to brighten the broth.

notes: Buy the pipis the day you cook and keep them on ice. Tap any open shells, they should close; if they don't, discard them.
You can make this with mussels or littleneck clams if you can't find pipis.
Food safety: Cook mussels and clams only if they are alive and tightly closed (or close when tapped), and throw out any that stay shut after cooking.

title: Taro and Pisupo Bake
summary: Taro root layered with corned beef and coconut cream, baked until tender and rich.

items.raw: 1.5 kg taro, peeled and sliced into 5 mm rounds
items.prep: peeled and sliced into 5 mm rounds

items.raw: 400 g tin corned beef, broken into chunks

steps.text: Heat oven to 180°C. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the corned beef to the pan and stir to break it up and warm through, about 3 minutes. Season with salt and white pepper.
In a large baking dish (about 30 × 20 cm), layer half the taro slices in an even layer. Top with the corned beef mixture, then layer the remaining taro slices on top.
Pour the coconut cream evenly over the top, making sure to reach the edges. Cover the dish tightly with foil.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the taro is completely tender when pierced with a fork and the coconut cream has been absorbed and the top is light golden.
Remove the foil and serve hot.

notes: Pisua is a great make-ahead dish, prepare it and refrigerate for up to a day, then bake when needed (add 10 minutes to cooking time).
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days and are even better reheated gently in a warm oven.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Rabo de Toro
summary: Rich Andalusian oxtail stew, slow-cooked with tomatoes, wine and warm spices.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or cazuela over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the oxtail pieces all over, about 3 minutes per side. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onions and carrots over medium heat, stirring often, for about 8 minutes. Add the crushed garlic, cumin and smoked paprika, and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the sherry and scrape the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Let it bubble gently for 2 minutes.

Return the oxtail to the pot and add the crushed tomatoes, beef stock and bay leaf. Bring to a simmer, season with salt and pepper, then cover and transfer to a 160°C oven for 3 hours, or until the meat is very tender and falls from the bone.
Remove from the oven, taste, and adjust seasoning. Skim any excess fat from the surface if you like. Serve hot with crusty bread, scattered with fresh parsley if you have it.

notes: This is even better made a day ahead. Cool, refrigerate overnight, then gently reheat. The flavours deepen and the fat is easy to lift off the cold surface.
Serve with crusty bread to soak up the sauce, and a simple green salad or steamed greens on the side.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Corned Beef Silog
summary: Canned corned beef with onions, garlic rice and fried eggs, the lazy silog when you're running late.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add the minced garlic and fry, stirring constantly, until fragrant and golden, about 1 minute. Add the chilled rice, breaking up any clumps, and stir-fry until heated through and grains are separated, about 4–5 minutes. Season with salt. Transfer to a serving plate and keep warm.
In the same pan or a fresh one, heat 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 3 minutes.

Add the corned beef straight from the tin, breaking it up with a spoon as it cooks. Stir-fry until the meat is heated through and lightly browned, about 4–5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

In a separate small pan, heat 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Crack both eggs into the pan and fry sunny-side up or over-easy until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny, about 3–4 minutes. Season lightly with salt.
Divide the garlic rice between two plates. Top each with the fried corned beef mixture and one fried egg. Serve immediately while the rice and egg are still warm.

notes: Use day-old rice for the best texture, fresh rice tends to clump when fried.
The corned beef tin is already cooked, so you're just heating and browning it for flavour.
Swap the fried egg for a sunny-side up or poached egg if you like, but that runny yolk over everything is the proper way to do it.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Chili Oil Chicken
summary: Poached chicken in aromatic chili oil with Sichuan peppercorns and fresh herbs.

items.raw: 1 whole chicken, about 1.5 kg, cut into pieces
2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm pieces
4 dried red chillies, halved and deseeded
Fresh chives, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Bring the 6 cups water to a boil in a large pot. Add the spring onion pieces, ginger slices, smashed garlic and salt. Simmer for 2 minutes to infuse the broth.

Add the chicken pieces to the simmering broth and return to a gentle boil. Skim any scum that rises. Reduce heat to a low simmer and poach until the chicken is cooked through (check the thickest pieces reach 75°C inside), about 15 minutes. Remove the chicken to a plate and let cool slightly, then shred or cut into bite-sized pieces. Discard the poaching liquid.

While the chicken cooks, make the chili oil. Heat the neutral oil in a small pan over medium heat. When it shimmers, add the Sichuan peppercorns and dried chillies. Toast, stirring gently, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and the oil is a deep amber, do not let it smoke or burn.

Remove the pan from heat. Add the doubanjiang, sliced garlic, sliced ginger, star anise and cinnamon stick. Stir well and let it infuse for 1 minute off the heat. The residual heat will open the flavours without charring them. Taste and add salt to balance.
Arrange the shredded chicken on a serving plate. Pour the warm chili oil (including the aromatics and spices) over the chicken.
Scatter with fresh coriander, chives, sliced spring onion and black sesame seeds if using. Serve warm or at room temperature with steamed rice.

notes: The chicken can be cooked and shredded up to 1 day ahead; reheat gently in a low oven before plating. The chili oil keeps in a clean glass jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks, use it on tofu, greens, or noodles.

Doubanjiang is spicy fermented bean paste from Sichuan; if you can't find it, skip this step rather than substituting, as it's essential to the flavour. Without it, this becomes a different (still good, but different) dish.
The numbing comes from the Sichuan peppercorns, not heat. If you prefer less mala, reduce them to 2 tablespoons.
Food safety: Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches 75°C and the juices run clear, with no pink meat near the bone.

title: Pig's Blood Cake
summary: Grilled QQ rice cakes with blood cake inside, coated in peanut powder and coriander.

items.raw: 300 g tinned pig's blood cake, cut into 2 cm cubes
200 g glutinous rice cake (mochi), cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Mix the soy sauce, sesame oil and white pepper in a small bowl.

Heat a little oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches so they fit in one layer, grill the blood cake cubes for 2 minutes on each side until the edges are golden and crispy, then set aside on a plate.
In the same pan, grill the glutinous rice cake cubes, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until they're golden and the outside is just starting to char while the inside stays QQ (soft and chewy).
Toss both the blood cake and rice cake with the soy sauce mixture.
Transfer to a plate and coat with the peanut powder and fresh coriander. Serve warm.

title: Gatsby
summary: Cape Town's legendary split loaf stuffed with fried chips, meat sauce and cheese

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot or deep fryer to 180°C. Fry the potato chips in batches until golden and crispy, about 4 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towel and season with salt while still hot.
Meanwhile, heat a tbsp of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned through, about 5–6 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste, cumin, coriander and chilli powder, cooking for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the beef stock and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and coats the back of a spoon, about 8–10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Lightly butter the inside of each bread roll. Warm the rolls under the griller or in a hot oven for 1–2 minutes until soft.
Layer the hot chips into each roll, then spoon the meat sauce generously over the top. Scatter the grated cheddar on top and place under the griller for 2–3 minutes until the cheese melts.
Serve immediately while hot and the cheese is still melted.

notes: You can prep the meat sauce ahead and reheat it just before assembling.
If you don't have a deep fryer, use a deep heavy-based pan with at least 8 cm of oil. Use a thermometer to check the temperature.
Some Cape Town versions add sliced cheese or a fried egg, feel free to customize.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Cook mince, sausages, meatballs and liver right through to 75°C, with no pink in the centre.

title: Cendol
summary: Sweet green rice flour noodles in coconut milk and palm sugar syrup.

items.raw: Pandan leaves, 3 or 4 leaves, tied in a knot (for colour and flavour)
items.prep: 3 or 4 leaves, tied in a knot

steps.text: Make the syrup first: In a small saucepan, combine the palm sugar and 200 ml water. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves completely, about 5 minutes. You should have a thick, smooth golden syrup. Remove from the heat and let it cool to room temperature.

Make the cendol batter: In a bowl, mix the rice flour, 200 ml water, salt and the pandan leaves together, stirring until smooth and lump-free. The batter should be thin, like condensed milk in consistency. Remove the pandan leaves and set the batter aside.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil (about 2 litres). Place the cendol maker (a special mould with holes, or use a sieve with small holes) over the boiling water. Working in batches, pour the batter slowly through the mould so the thin noodles drop straight into the boiling water. They will sink at first, then float to the surface in about 1 minute, that is when they are cooked.
Remove the cooked cendol with a slotted spoon and place them immediately into a bowl of ice-cold water to stop the cooking. Drain well and set aside. Repeat with the remaining batter.
In a small saucepan, warm the coconut milk gently over low heat until steaming, do not let it boil. Add a pinch of salt and stir. Let it cool to room temperature.

To serve, divide the cendol noodles among four glasses or bowls, pour a little of the palm sugar syrup over them (about 50 ml per serving), then pour the cooled coconut milk on top (about 100 ml per serving). Fill each glass with ice and serve immediately, ice-cold.

notes: If you don't have a proper cendol maker, use a fine sieve or even a ladle with small holes; the noodles don't need to be perfect, just thin.
Everything must be ice-cold before serving, chill the glasses if you want to be proper about it.

title: Gado-Gado Bali
summary: Mixed vegetables with rich peanut sauce tempered by base genep and palm sugar.

items.raw: 1 cm piece fresh galangal, roughly chopped
150 g long bean, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Grind the garlic, shallots, chillies, turmeric and galangal together with a mortar and pestle (or in a food processor) until you have a fine paste. This is your base genep.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the base genep and cook, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant.
Grind the roasted peanuts finely. Add to the pan along with the palm sugar, tamarind paste and coconut milk. Stir well and simmer for 3 to 4 minutes. Taste and adjust salt.

Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the cabbage and long beans, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until tender-crisp. Add the bean sprouts and spinach, and cook for a further 1 to 2 minutes until just wilted. Drain well.
Add the cooked vegetables to the peanut sauce and toss gently to coat. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The base genep can be made a day ahead and stored in an airtight container in the fridge.
Gado-gado tastes equally good warm, room temperature, or even chilled the next day.

title: Ikan Sambal Matah
summary: Pan-fried white fish topped with a sharp raw sambal of shallots, garlic and bird's eye chillies.

items.raw: 2–3 bird's eye chillies, finely sliced (adjust to taste)
800 g white fish fillets (barramundi, snapper or similar), skin on

steps.text: Make the sambal: combine the shallots, garlic, chillies, lime juice, oil and salt in a bowl. Taste and adjust the heat or salt as needed. Leave it at room temperature while you cook the fish.
Pat the fish dry with paper towel and season both sides with salt.
Heat a little oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When it's hot, add the fish skin-side down and cook without moving it until the skin is crispy and golden, about 4–5 minutes.
Flip the fish carefully and cook the other side until just cooked through, about 2–3 minutes. The fish is done when it flakes easily with a fork.
Transfer the fish to a serving plate and spoon the sambal matah generously over the top. Scatter with coriander if you like, and serve with lime wedges on the side.

notes: The sambal can be made up to 2 hours ahead; keep it at room temperature so the flavours stay fresh and sharp.
Any firm white fish works here. Adjust cooking time by a minute or two depending on thickness.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Kongnamul Muchim
summary: Warm soybean sprouts with toasted sesame oil and ginger, nutty and grounding.

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to the boil and blanch the bean sprouts for 3 minutes until just tender but still bright. Drain well and squeeze gently with your hands to remove excess moisture.
In a large bowl, combine the warm sprouts with the sesame oil, ginger, and salt. Toss gently until the sprouts are evenly coated.
Transfer to a serving plate and scatter the toasted sesame seeds over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature as part of a Korean meal.

notes: This banchan keeps for up to three days refrigerated. It's equally good cold, straight from the bowl.
The quality of your sesame oil matters here, use a good toasted variety for the full nutty flavour.

title: Cơm Tấm Sườn Nướng
summary: Saigon broken rice with grilled pork chop, fried egg and caramelised fish sauce.

items.raw: 2 pork loin chops, about 200 g each

steps.text: Make the fish sauce caramel: add sugar to a small pan over medium heat. Once golden, about 2 minutes, add fish sauce slowly (it will bubble), then stir in the garlic and chilli. Remove from heat and set aside.
Marinate the pork: mix fish sauce, sugar, garlic and black pepper. Coat the chops well and leave for at least 15 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Cook the broken rice: rinse in a sieve, then cook in boiling salted water, about 12 minutes, until tender but with a slight bite. Drain well and set aside.

Grill or pan-fry the pork: heat 1 tbsp oil in a heavy-based pan over high heat until smoking. Cook the chops, without moving them, for 3 to 4 minutes until the edges char. Flip and cook for another 3 to 4 minutes (they should still be slightly pink inside). Rest for 5 minutes, then slice.
Fry the eggs: in the same pan, heat a little more oil and fry the eggs until the whites are set but the yolks soft, about 3 minutes.
Assemble: divide the rice between two bowls, top with sliced pork, a fried egg, cucumber and pickled vegetables if using. Drizzle with fish sauce caramel, scatter spring onion and serve.

notes: The broken rice should have a slight bite, don't overcook it. If you can't find it, use jasmine rice but reduce the cooking time to 10 minutes.
Make the fish sauce caramel up to a day ahead and store in a jar; reheat gently before serving.
Pickled daikon and carrot (cà chua cà rốt) from the supermarket are traditional but optional, they add a salty, vinegary edge.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Larb Het
summary: Northern Thai mushroom larb with lime, herbs and toasted rice powder.

items.raw: 400 g mixed mushrooms (button, shiitake, oyster), finely chopped

steps.text: Toast 2 tbsp white rice in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Tip into a mortar and pestle or spice grinder, and grind to a coarse powder. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped mushrooms and cook, stirring often, until they soften and release their liquid, about 5 minutes. The mushrooms should be tender and any liquid should have mostly evaporated.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the lime juice, tamari, toasted rice powder and sliced onion. Taste and adjust the lime, tamari or chilli to your preference.
Transfer to a serving plate. Tear over the coriander and mint, and serve with cos lettuce leaves to wrap, if you like.

notes: Make the toasted rice powder ahead and keep it in a jar, it will keep for weeks and makes larb het much quicker on the day.
Larb het is best served at room temperature or warm. It doesn't keep well, so make it just before you want to eat.

title: Atsuage
summary: Thick-fried tofu cutlet with dashi and grated daikon.

items.raw: 300 g firm tofu, drained and cut into 2 thick slices
items.prep: drained and cut into 2 thick slices

steps.text: Pat the tofu slices dry with paper towels. Blot both sides well, this is important for crispy frying.

Heat about 3 cm of oil in a small, deep pan to 160°C. The tofu will sink and then float as it cooks; if you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden chopstick, bubbles should form steadily around it.
Carefully lower the tofu into the hot oil. Fry for 4 minutes until the surface is golden and crispy, then gently turn it over and fry for another 4 minutes until both sides are golden.
Warm the dashi in a small saucepan. Stir in the soy sauce and mirin.
Transfer the hot tofu to a bowl. Pour the hot dashi over it. Top with the grated daikon and spring onion. Eat while it's still steaming.

notes: The key is drying the tofu well before frying, squeeze it gently between clean cloths to release as much water as you can.
Atsuage is best eaten straight away, while the outside is still crackling and the inside soft.

title: Kanji Vada
summary: Crispy lentil fritters soaked in spiced carrot pickle and mustard oil.

items.raw: 1 cup urad dal (white lentils), soaked for 30 minutes
500 g carrot, cut into thin sticks
4 dried red chillies, broken into pieces

steps.text: Make the kanji first. Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it just smokes, then remove from heat. When it has cooled to warm, add the mustard seeds, fenugreek seeds, and dried chillies. Let them crackle for a few seconds, then stir in the asafoetida. In a jar, combine the carrot sticks with salt, then pour the hot oil and spices over them. Add the citric acid, stir well, and set aside to cool completely.
Drain the urad dal and grind it to a thick, smooth paste using a wet grinder or food processor, adding just a splash of water if needed, the batter should be light and fluffy, not wet.
Transfer the batter to a bowl. Fold in the rice flour, green chilli, cumin seeds, and salt, mixing gently to keep the batter airy.
Heat the oil for frying in a large, heavy pan to 180°C (a small piece of batter should sizzle and rise to the top immediately).

Wet your fingers and shape small balls of batter about the size of a walnut, then gently slide them into the hot oil. Fry in batches until golden and crisp all over, being careful not to crowd the pan.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring gently and turning the vada so they brown evenly. They should be golden and crispy. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Once the vada have cooled to room temperature, add them to the kanji jar and mix gently so each one is coated with the pickle. Cover and leave for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: The kanji keeps in the fridge for up to 10 days, and the vada soften into it beautifully.
If you don't have a wet grinder, a good blender works fine, just be patient and add water slowly so the batter stays light.

title: Abgoosht
summary: Persian meat and chickpea broth served two ways: the broth first, then pounded solids on bread.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 4 large chunks
400 g tinned chickpeas, drained and rinsed
3 medium waxy potatoes, peeled and halved
Fresh herbs (coriander or parsley), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef chunks on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Don't rush this step.
Add the onions and turmeric, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim any foam from the surface until the liquid looks clear. Add the black pepper and a pinch of salt.
Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 45 minutes.
Add the potatoes and chickpeas, and simmer, covered, for another 45 minutes until the meat is very tender and the broth is rich and deep in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. You should have a clear, flavourful broth and very soft solids.
To serve, ladle the broth into bowls as the first course. Pour the remaining broth over the meat and vegetables.

Pound the cooked meat and potatoes with a wooden spoon or potato masher directly in the pot until roughly crushed. Pile onto toasted bread, drizzle with a little broth, and serve as the second course. Garnish with fresh herbs if you have them.

notes: This is traditionally made in a heavy pot called a dizi. An enamelled cast iron or stainless steel pot works just as well.
Some cooks add dried limes (loomi) or a pinch of saffron for extra depth. This version keeps it simple.
The broth keeps well for 3 days in the fridge, and tastes even better the next day.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Rad Na Gai
summary: Silky tapioca gravy over soft noodles and chicken, a one-burner Bangkok dinner.

items.raw: 2 tbsp tapioca starch, mixed with 3 tbsp water

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the egg noodles until soft, about 3–4 minutes, stirring gently to prevent sticking. Drain and tip into a bowl.
In the same pot (no need to rinse), heat the oil over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and fry gently until fragrant and golden, about 1 minute, don't burn it.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer until the sauce is bubbling gently. Add the soy sauce and sugar, then taste. Adjust salt and white pepper to your liking.

Stir the tapioca starch mixture to recombine it (it will have settled), then slowly pour it into the simmering stock while stirring constantly. Keep stirring for 1–2 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns glossy and translucent.
Add the shredded chicken and stir to heat through, about 1 minute. The gravy should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon but still pour easily.
Place the soft noodles in a bowl and carefully pour the hot gravy over them. Top with fried garlic, fresh coriander if you have it, and pickled chilli if you like heat. Eat while it's hot.

notes: Cook from leftover rotisserie chicken or use tinned tuna (drained) for a different angle.
The gravy thickens as it cools slightly, aim for thick but pourable at the stove.
Scale up easily: double the stock and starch for two bowls, cook noodles separately.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Miso Soup with Hamaguri
summary: Delicate clam miso soup, a weekend breakfast ritual

items.raw: Small piece fresh ginger, peeled and sliced thinly (optional)

steps.text: Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer in a pot until tiny bubbles rise at the edges.
Add the cleaned clams and a thin slice of ginger if using. Cover and simmer until the clams just begin to open, 3 to 4 minutes.
Scoop the clams into serving bowls as they open (don't wait for all of them; they open in stages).
Dissolve the white miso in a small bowl with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then pour it back into the pot. Stir gently, do not let the broth boil or the miso flavour will flatten.
Add the mirin to the pot and taste. Add a small pinch of salt if needed.
Pour the broth over the clams in each bowl, scatter the spring onion on top, and serve immediately.

notes: Clean the clams by scrubbing them under cold water and soaking in salted water for an hour if you have time; this helps them expel sand.
Make-ahead: prepare the dashi and have the clams cleaned and ready the night before. The soup itself takes just 15 minutes on the day.
If clams are very large, you can halve them after opening for easier eating.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking.

title: Chupe de Camarones
summary: Creamy Peruvian shrimp and potato chowder with ají amarillo and fresh cheese.

items.raw: 600 g waxy potato, peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

items.raw: 400 g raw prawns, peeled and deveined
150 g fresh mozzarella (or quesillo), torn or cubed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in garlic and ají amarillo paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in stock and bring to a simmer. Add potato and capsicum, then stir in cumin. Cook for 12–15 minutes, until potato is just tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Add prawns and cook, stirring gently, until they turn opaque and firm, about 3–4 minutes. Do not overcook.
Remove from heat. Divide fresh cheese among serving bowls, then ladle the hot chupe over it, the cheese will soften and melt into the broth.
Top each bowl with two egg halves and garnish with coriander if you like. Serve immediately.

notes: You can make the broth a day ahead; store it in the fridge and add the prawns just before serving.
Quesillo or fresh mozzarella works best here, it melts into silken clouds in the hot broth. Avoid hard cheeses.
If you can't find ají amarillo paste, substitute 2 tsp of ají amarillo powder mixed with a little water.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Dhal and Jaggery
summary: Creamy red lentil curry with coconut and a touch of jaggery sweetness.

steps.text: Rinse the lentils under cold water until the water runs clear. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger and red chilli, stirring constantly, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the ground coriander and turmeric, cooking for another 30 seconds.
Add the rinsed lentils and water, bringing to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils begin to break down.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir well. Continue to cook for another 10 minutes, stirring often, until the lentils are completely soft and the curry is creamy.
Stir in the palm sugar and salt to taste. Cook for 2 more minutes, then taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. The curry should be creamy, not thick; add a little warm water if it's too dense.

notes: Keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
Serve with steamed rice, hoppers or roti to soak up the sauce.
Food safety: Reheat leftovers until steaming hot right through.

title: Jaew Makhuea Thet (Charred Tomato Jaew)
summary: Smoky charred tomato and chilli dip with lime and fish sauce.

items.raw: 2–3 birds eye chillies (adjust to your heat)

steps.text: If you have a gas stove, char the tomatoes, chillies and garlic directly over the flame, turning with tongs, until blackened and soft all over, about 10–12 minutes. If you only have electric, use a grill pan or cast iron over high heat, turning often, until deeply charred. The darker the better.
Let cool for a minute, then peel away the charred skin from the tomatoes and discard. Peel the garlic cloves.
Pound the charred tomatoes, chillies and garlic in a mortar and pestle until you have a rough paste, it should be chunky, not smooth.
Stir in the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and add salt if needed. The dip should be smoky, hot and sharp all at once.

notes: Serve with sticky rice, grilled chicken, prawns or crispy pork, and plenty of fresh vegetables.
You can make it an hour ahead and it keeps fine in the fridge, but the smokiness is best fresh.

title: Chapli Kebab
summary: Spiced minced lamb kebab with pomegranate seeds and fresh herbs, crispy outside and juicy within.

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the lamb mince, pomegranate seeds, green chilli, onion, garlic, fresh coriander, mint and egg. Add the ground cumin, ground coriander, chilli powder, garam masala and salt. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the kebabs will be dense.
Divide the mixture into 8 equal portions. Wet your hands lightly and shape each portion into a thick oval, pressing gently but firmly so it holds together.
Heat a large frying pan or tawa over medium-high heat and add 2 tbsp oil. Once shimmering, carefully place 4 kebabs in the pan without crowding.

Cook for 5 to 6 minutes on the first side until golden brown and crispy, then flip carefully. Cook for another 3 to 4 minutes until the second side is golden and the meat is cooked through (the internal temperature should reach 75°C).
Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate and cook the remaining 4 kebabs in the same way, adding a little more oil if needed, until each is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges.
Serve hot with lemon wedges, sliced onions and yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a lined tray, covered.
For extra crunch, add 2 tbsp finely chopped pistachios or almonds to the mince.
Serve with naan or flatbread, sliced onions, lemon and a dollop of cooling yoghurt.
Food safety: Cook mince, sausages, meatballs and liver right through to 75°C, with no pink in the centre.

title: Wattleseed Shortbread
summary: Buttery shortbread with wattleseed flour and a hint of lemon myrtle.

steps.text: Preheat your camp oven (or conventional oven to 180°C) with a tray inside.
Cream butter and caster sugar together in a bowl until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes.
In another bowl, whisk together plain flour, wattleseed flour and lemon myrtle if using.
Fold the dry ingredients into the butter mixture until a soft dough forms.
Transfer dough to a sheet of baking paper. Press into a 20 cm square (about 1 cm thick), prick lightly with a fork, and scatter flaky salt over the top.
Slide onto the hot tray in the camp oven and bake for 18–22 minutes, until pale golden at the edges but still soft in the middle.
Remove from oven and let cool on the tray for 5 minutes, then cut into 12 pieces while still warm.
Cool completely on a wire rack before serving.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days.
You can make this in a conventional oven at 180°C if you don't have a camp oven, bake for 18–20 minutes.
If you can't find wattleseed flour locally, use the same weight of plain flour instead, though you'll lose the earthy, distinctive flavour.

title: Lentil Ladera
summary: Brown lentils braised in tomato and onion until they become their own sauce.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Rinse the lentils well under cold water and pick through for any stones. Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until very soft and golden, about 10 minutes. The onion should be completely tender.
Stir in the lentils and cook for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes and oregano. Stir well to combine.
Add 750 ml of water and bring to a simmer. Reduce heat to low and cook, stirring occasionally, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the lentils are very soft and beginning to break down.
The lentils should create their own sauce as they cook and soften. If the mixture becomes too thick, add a little more water. If it's too thin, let it simmer uncovered for a few minutes longer.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

title: Lentil and Rice Soup
summary: Creamy, warming soup of brown lentils and rice with cumin and garlic, weeknight dinner that costs almost nothing.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cumin seeds, and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Tip in the lentils and rice, stir to coat with oil, and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer, uncovered, for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils and rice are very soft and the soup is thick and creamy.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. If it's too thick, add a splash of water. Serve hot.

notes: Leftover soup keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen.
You can use any lentils you've got, red lentils will make it even creamier but break down faster, so check it at 20 minutes.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Mboga ya Managu
summary: Sautéed amaranth greens with tomatoes and onions

steps.text: Wash the amaranth greens well and roughly chop them.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with a spoon. Simmer for 3 minutes.
Add the chopped greens, salt and pepper. Stir well to combine. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and cooked through, about 6 minutes. The mixture should be saucy but not soupy.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot with ugali or rice.

title: Grilled Fish Wrapped in Vine Leaves
summary: Whole fish sealed in grape leaves on the charcoal, herbs and lemon steam inside.

items.raw: 2 whole white fish (400 g each), gutted and cleaned
12 grape vine leaves, rinsed and patted dry

steps.text: Light your charcoal and let it burn down to glowing coals. You want heat, not flame.
Pat the fish dry inside and out. Season the cavity with salt, pepper and a pinch of oregano. Stuff each fish with 2 lemon slices and 1 oregano sprig.

Lay 6 vine leaves on a work surface, overlapping them to form a base. Place a fish on top, then fold the leaves up and around it, tucking and overlapping to seal it completely. Do the same with the other fish.
Brush each parcel lightly with olive oil. Place on the grill grate over the coals and cook until the leaves are charred and the fish flakes easily and is opaque inside.

Cook for 10–12 minutes until the vine leaves are charred black on top. Flip the parcel carefully, then cook for another 8–10 minutes on the other side until the second side is charred and the fish is cooked through (the flesh should be opaque and flake easily at the thickest part).
Slide onto a plate and let rest for 2 minutes. Unwrap at the table. The leaves are burnt, but the fish inside is perfect, steamed in its own juices with lemon and herb.

notes: Use jarred vine leaves if fresh aren't available. Rinse off the brine and pat dry.
Any whole white fish works: bream, snapper, flathead. Aim for 350–450 g per fish.
The blackened leaves are not meant to be eaten. Unwrap carefully and discard.
Food safety: Cook fish until it turns opaque and flakes easily, about 63°C in the thickest part.

title: Lamb and Cumin Hand-Pulled Noodles
summary: Chewy hand-pulled noodles tossed with cumin-spiced lamb, a Western Chinese favourite.

items.raw: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for kneading

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Pour in warm water and 2 tbsp oil, stirring with your fingers until it comes together into a shaggy mass. Knead on a lightly oiled bench for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel slightly tacky but not sticky. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

While the dough rests, cook the lamb: heat oil in a wok or large frying pan over high heat. Add lamb, breaking it up with a spoon, and cook until just cooked through and starting to colour, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, ground cumin and cumin seeds, stirring constantly for 1 minute until fragrant. Add chilli flakes and spring onions, cooking for another minute.
Pour in soy sauce and black vinegar, tossing everything together. Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Transfer to a serving bowl and keep warm.

Divide rested dough into 4 equal pieces. Working with one piece at a time, use your hands to stretch it gently, then hold it up and let gravity help pull it into a long, thin noodle. If it springs back, rest it for a minute and try again. Lay stretched noodle on a floured bench and repeat with remaining dough pieces.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Add noodles one at a time, stirring gently. Once water returns to boil, cook for 2–3 minutes until chewy and cooked through. Drain well.
Toss hot noodles with the warm lamb mixture and serve immediately in bowls.

notes: The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If you're short on time, you can stretch the noodles thinner and cook them a little faster, just watch they don't break.
You can use beef mince instead of lamb; the cumin-to-meat ratio stays the same. Some cooks add a handful of fresh coriander or a drizzle of chilli oil to finish.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Kokotxas en Salsa Verde
summary: Hake jowls in a silky parsley sauce, expensive, delicate, worth every euro.

items.raw: 30 g fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped

steps.text: Put the kokotxas in a wide, shallow pan with the white wine and fish stock. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 3 to 4 minutes, until just cooked through, they should be opaque but still delicate. Carefully transfer the kokotxas to a warm plate with a slotted spoon, keeping the cooking liquid in the pan.
Heat the olive oil in another pan over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, until it is just starting to soften and colour, about 2 minutes. Do not burn it.
Pour the cooking liquid (about 300 ml) into the pan with the garlic and oil, and bring to a simmer. Add the chopped parsley and cook for 1 minute.

In a small bowl, beat the egg yolks lightly. Remove the pan from the heat, let it cool for 30 seconds, then slowly pour in the egg yolks while whisking constantly, this makes the sauce silky and rich without scrambling the eggs. Taste and season with salt and white pepper.
Gently return the kokotxas to the pan and warm through for 30 seconds without letting the sauce boil, until the fish is just opaque and the sauce is glossy.
Divide among four bowls, pour the salsa verde over and around the kokotxas, and serve with crusty bread to soak up every drop.

notes: Kokotxas are expensive and seasonal. Buy them very fresh from a good fishmonger, or ask them to order them in.
The sauce must never boil after the egg yolks are added, or it will scramble. Keep the heat low.
Don't skip the white pepper, it's gentler than black and won't speckle the delicate pale sauce.
Food safety: Cook fish until it turns opaque and flakes easily, about 63°C in the thickest part.

title: Fideuà
summary: Crispy short noodles with seafood, toasted and socarrat-crunchy at the bottom.

items.raw: 300 g short thin noodles (fideuà or thin spaghetti broken into 3 cm pieces)
items.note: fideuà or thin spaghetti broken into 3 cm pieces

items.raw: 400 ml seafood stock (or fish stock), warm
1 tsp saffron threads, soaked in 60 ml warm water
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the aioli first: in a mortar or small bowl, pound the garlic with a pinch of salt until smooth. Add the egg yolk and stir well. Add the oil a drop at a time, whisking constantly, until it begins to emulsify. Once thickened, add the oil in a thin stream, whisking continuously. Finish with lemon juice and salt. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a paella pan or large shallow frying pan (about 30 cm) over medium heat. Add the noodles and toast, stirring often, until they turn golden and fragrant, about 3 to 4 minutes. Remove and set aside.

In the same pan, heat a little more oil if needed and soften the onion, garlic and capsicum over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. This sofregit should be slow and gentle, don't rush it.
Add the tomato and cook for 2 minutes, stirring.

Return the toasted noodles to the pan and stir to coat. Pour in the warm stock and the saffron with its soaking water. Bring to a simmer and cook without stirring for about 10 minutes, until most of the liquid has been absorbed and the noodles are tender.

Scatter the prawns and squid over the top, season with salt and pepper, and continue cooking for about 5 minutes, stirring gently, until the prawns are cooked through (opaque and firm) and the squid is tender.
Increase the heat to medium-high for the last minute to create the socarrat, listen for a gentle crackling sound from the bottom. Don't burn it; you want a dark, crispy crust, not black.
Remove from heat. Scatter with fresh parsley and serve straight from the pan with the aioli on the side.

notes: If you can't find fideuà noodles, break thin spaghetti or vermicelli into short pieces before toasting.
The socarrat is crucial, that dark, crackling crust at the bottom. Listen for it; don't walk away during those last 30 seconds.
Make the aioli ahead if you like; it keeps in the fridge for a day.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Mizeria
summary: Crisp cucumber salad in cool sour cream and fresh dill, the Polish summer side dish for everything.

items.raw: 4 medium cucumbers, peeled, halved lengthways and sliced thin
items.prep: peeled, halved lengthways and sliced thin

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh dill, chopped (or 1 tsp dried dill)
2 tbsp apple cider vinegar (or white vinegar)
